set-01-A-001.why: Most left-ventricular coronary inflow occurs during diastole because systolic muscle contraction compresses intramural vessels. Local metabolic vasodilatation increases flow when myocardial oxygen demand outstrips delivery.

notes.A: Contraction of ventricular muscle compresses left coronary vessels early in systole and reduces inflow, especially in deeper wall layers.
notes.B: Myocardial hypoxia promotes release of local vasodilators, including adenosine, which increase flow if coronary reserve is available.
notes.C: Cooling typically lowers myocardial metabolic demand, reducing the stimulus for coronary vasodilatation and increased flow.
notes.D: A rise in heart rate and contractility raises myocardial oxygen demand. Local metabolic vasodilatation generally increases flow despite direct adrenergic effects.
notes.E: Within the autoregulatory range, coronary resistance changes with perfusion pressure and keeps steady-state flow relatively constant.

set-01-A-002.why: Ventricular filling begins when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure and the atrioventricular valves open. Rapid passive filling occurs first, with atrial contraction contributing near end-diastole.

notes.A: Most filling at a normal resting rate is passive. Atrial contraction adds a variable portion near the end of diastole.
notes.B: During isovolumetric relaxation inflow and outflow valves are closed. Filling starts only once an atrioventricular valve opens.
notes.C: Rapid early filling can produce an audible third heart sound, which may be physiological in young people or pregnancy.
notes.D: The atrium need only exceed the ventricle in pressure. Absolute pressure relative to the atmosphere does not determine valve opening.
notes.E: The atrioventricular pressure gradient is initially greatest in early diastole, and filling slows later during diastasis.

set-01-A-004.why: Fluid filtration increases when capillary hydrostatic pressure rises or plasma oncotic pressure falls. Lymphatic return normally clears filtered fluid, so failure of drainage can cause accumulation independently.

notes.A: Arteriolar dilatation transmits more pressure to downstream capillaries and increases the outward hydrostatic driving force.
notes.B: Standing adds a gravitational pressure head to vessels below the heart, raising venous and capillary pressure in the legs.
notes.C: Lymphatic blockage primarily prevents return of filtered fluid and protein. The resulting oedema does not require an immediate increase in capillary filtration.
notes.D: A venous obstruction raises upstream venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure, promoting outward fluid transfer.
notes.E: Lower albumin reduces the plasma oncotic force opposing filtration and favours net fluid loss from capillaries.

set-01-A-005.why: As an upper-arm cuff deflates, the first Korotkoff sounds mark systolic pressure and their disappearance usually marks diastolic pressure. The correct cuff size helps avoid systematic error.

notes.A: The pulse distends the partly compressed brachial artery and generates vibrations in nearby tissue. The sounds arise locally.
notes.B: The first tapping sounds appear as cuff pressure falls just below peak arterial pressure and intermittent flow resumes.
notes.C: Diastolic pressure usually corresponds to disappearance of the sounds. The loudest phase is not the standard endpoint.
notes.D: A palpable distal pulse may return only after some flow is restored. An auscultatory gap can also cause error if missed.
notes.E: A larger arm needs a proportionately larger cuff bladder. A cuff that is too small can overestimate pressure.

set-01-A-006.why: Vascular resistance depends strongly on lumen radius and also on blood viscosity and vessel length. Arteriolar smooth muscle changes resistance dynamically by changing lumen size.

notes.A: For ideal laminar flow in a tube, resistance varies inversely with radius to the fourth power. Halving radius increases resistance sixteenfold.
notes.B: Wall thickness affects mechanics, but it is the lumen radius that enters the basic resistance relation when other flow conditions are fixed.
notes.C: Contraction of vascular smooth muscle narrows the lumen and increases resistance. Relaxation tends to have the opposite effect.
notes.D: Higher viscosity increases resistance for a given vessel geometry because more pressure is needed to sustain the same flow.
notes.E: Each capillary has a narrow lumen, but many lie in parallel. Arterioles normally account for a larger pressure drop.

set-01-A-007.why: Central command and autonomic reflexes increase cardiac sympathetic drive during exercise, excitement and hypotension. A sudden arterial pressure rise activates baroreceptors and normally reduces that drive.

notes.A: Exercise raises sympathetic output, helping accelerate the cardiac pacemaker and increase ventricular contractile force.
notes.B: Excitement can activate central autonomic pathways and increase sympathetic stimulation of the heart.
notes.C: Hypotension reduces stretch and firing in arterial baroreceptors, increasing reflex sympathetic outflow to the heart.
notes.D: Limbic and hypothalamic activity can recruit medullary cardiovascular pathways during emotions, increasing adrenergic drive.
notes.E: A sudden pressure rise increases baroreceptor firing and typically decreases sympathetic drive while increasing cardiac vagal activity.

set-01-A-008.why: The electrocardiogram records electrical activation and recovery before their mechanical consequences. The PR interval includes atrioventricular conduction, while the QT interval spans ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation.

notes.A: Ventricular depolarisation produces the QRS complex and precedes force generation in the ventricular muscle.
notes.B: The T wave reflects the net electrical effect of ventricular repolarisation after the myocardium is activated.
notes.C: Atrial depolarisation is the P wave. The PR interval also includes conduction of the impulse toward the ventricles.
notes.D: From QRS onset to the end of the T wave, the QT interval approximates the period of ventricular electrical activity.
notes.E: In respiratory sinus arrhythmia, the rate usually rises during inspiration and falls during expiration as vagal activity varies.

set-01-A-009.why: Flow is more prone to turbulence when the Reynolds number rises. For a given velocity and vessel diameter, lower viscosity increases Reynolds number by weakening viscous damping.

notes.A: At fixed velocity, a smaller vessel diameter lowers Reynolds number. This makes turbulence less likely, other factors being equal.
notes.B: Lower density reduces inertial forces relative to viscous forces, decreasing Reynolds number at the same velocity and diameter.
notes.C: Slower flow reduces inertial forces relative to viscous forces and lowers the tendency toward turbulence.
notes.D: Lower viscosity provides less damping of flow disturbances and increases Reynolds number when other variables are held constant.
notes.E: Anaemia generally reduces blood viscosity and can increase flow velocity through higher cardiac output. Both changes favour flow murmurs.

set-01-B-001.why: Starting muscle length affects the active tension generated. Within the ascending part of the length–tension relation, stretching increases force, helping the heart match stroke volume to ventricular filling.

notes.A: Increased available calcium can raise force at a fixed length. That is a change in activation, not the length–tension relation.
notes.B: Active tension depends on initial length and eventually falls beyond an optimal range. It does not increase exponentially with stretch.
notes.D: Coronary perfusion supplies the myocardium with oxygen. It is ventricular filling that increases initial fibre stretch in the Starling response.
notes.E: Pressure against the muscle reflects its load. Greater load generally reduces shortening if initial length and activation are unchanged.

set-01-B-003.why: Sinoatrial pacemaker cells generate impulses intrinsically, so a denervated heart can keep beating and sustain circulation. Neural input normally adjusts its rate and force to demand.

notes.A: Pacemaker depolarisation is intrinsic to the sinoatrial node, so loss of extrinsic nerve supply does not stop the heart.
notes.C: Circulating catecholamines can still change rate in a denervated heart, although rapid neural control is lost.
notes.D: Removing neural input reduces the speed and range of autonomic adjustments. It does not inherently improve pumping efficiency.
notes.E: Heart sounds result from vibrations associated with mechanical events, especially valve closure, which continue in a beating denervated heart.

set-01-B-004.why: Cardiac output is the volume delivered by one ventricle per unit time, usually one minute. It equals stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.

notes.A: Work or energy transfer per minute describes power. Output here measures volume per time rather than energy per time.
notes.C: Opening the aorta would change pressures and circulatory conditions, so the resulting bleeding rate cannot define normal cardiac output.
notes.D: Cardiac output applies at rest and during exercise. The total volume also needs a specified time interval.
notes.E: The volume delivered by one ventricle to its circulation per minute gives the definition represented among the choices.

set-01-B-005.why: At the start of left ventricular systole, rising ventricular pressure closes the mitral valve. The aortic valve opens later, after ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure.

notes.A: The mitral valve closes before ventricular ejection. The aortic valve does not open until pressure builds sufficiently.
notes.C: An open mitral valve with a closed aortic valve is the usual filling configuration during ventricular diastole.
notes.D: Pressure differences determine valve position. The normal early systolic interval can be identified without information about sympathetic activity.
notes.E: Both valves are closed during isovolumetric contraction, allowing ventricular pressure to rise at constant chamber volume.

set-01-B-006.why: Gap junction channels allow depolarising current to pass between neighbouring ventricular myocytes. Their low-resistance coupling helps activation spread rapidly through myocardium after the conducting system delivers the impulse.

notes.B: Intercalated discs contain mechanical contacts as well as gap junctions. The gap junction channels specifically provide electrical coupling.
notes.C: Mitochondria supply metabolic energy for ion transport and contraction. They do not carry depolarising current into adjacent cells.
notes.D: The Golgi apparatus modifies and sorts proteins inside each cell. It does not provide a direct electrical route between cells.
notes.E: Sarcoplasmic reticulum releases calcium to activate contraction after depolarisation. It does not conduct the depolarisation from cell to cell.

set-01-B-007.why: Endothelin released by vascular endothelium generally constricts systemic resistance vessels by activating smooth muscle receptors. Local metabolites and nitric oxide often favour dilation instead.

notes.A: Carbon dioxide can accumulate in active tissue and contribute to local systemic vasodilatation, increasing perfusion to the area.
notes.B: A lower local pH often accompanies increased metabolism and can relax resistance vessels in systemic tissues.
notes.C: Local warming can increase cutaneous flow through vasodilatation, helping transfer excess heat to the surroundings.
notes.E: Endothelial nitric oxide activates soluble guanylate cyclase in vascular smooth muscle and promotes relaxation through cyclic GMP.

set-01-B-009.why: The heart creates the pressure gradients for pulmonary and systemic flow and also has sensory and endocrine functions. The systemic venous circulation contains the main blood-volume reservoir.

notes.A: Stretch of atrial myocytes promotes secretion of atrial natriuretic peptide, which supports sodium excretion by the kidneys.
notes.B: Ventricular contraction generates pressure differences that drive blood through pulmonary and systemic vascular beds.
notes.C: The atrial and ventricular septa form a barrier that separates the systemic and pulmonary blood streams in the normal heart.
notes.E: Atrial stretch receptors sense filling and participate in autonomic and endocrine responses to changes in blood volume.

set-01-B-010.why: Low alveolar oxygen causes constriction of nearby pulmonary arterioles. This response redirects blood away from poorly ventilated regions and helps match ventilation to perfusion.

notes.A: Pulmonary arteries carry mixed venous blood into the lungs. Pulmonary veins normally carry more oxygenated blood away.
notes.B: The myocardium extracts a large share of delivered oxygen, so coronary sinus blood usually has less oxygen than mixed venous blood.
notes.C: In steady state the ventricular flows are close. Bronchial venous drainage into the left heart can make left-sided flow slightly greater.
notes.E: In most systemic tissues, lower local oxygen favours arteriolar dilatation and increases blood flow to restore delivery.

set-01-B-011.why: Nodal cells, conducting fibres and working myocardial cells all generate electrical activity. Surface ECG chiefly represents summed myocardial activity, while specialised conduction signals can be recorded intracardially.

notes.A: Sinoatrial cells produce spontaneous pacemaker action potentials that normally set heart rate.
notes.B: Atrioventricular nodal cells produce action potentials and carry impulses slowly between atria and ventricles.
notes.C: Activation of atrial and ventricular working myocytes provides much of the deflection measured on the body surface.
notes.D: The bundle of His conducts impulses toward the bundle branches. Its local electrical signal can be recorded intracardially.

set-01-B-012.why: Cardiac excitation spreads through electrically coupled myocytes rather than recruiting skeletal motor units. Ventricular force varies with initial fibre length and calcium availability to the myofilaments.

notes.B: Greater filling stretches cardiac muscle and can increase stroke volume through the Frank–Starling mechanism within the physiological range.
notes.C: The cytosolic calcium transient depends partly on sarcoplasmic reticulum release. Changing that transient can alter the strength of contraction.
notes.D: Positive inotropic agents increase force at a given initial muscle length, reflecting enhanced contractility.
notes.E: Adrenaline stimulates cardiac beta-1 receptors and increases calcium availability, strengthening ventricular contraction.

set-01-B-014.why: In a typical narrow systemic capillary, red blood cells pass in single file. Their deformable membranes allow them to squeeze through lumens comparable to, or smaller than, their resting diameter.

notes.B: Two erythrocytes can be present at different points along a capillary, but the typical lumen is too narrow for them to pass side by side.
notes.C: Three cells abreast need a wider lumen than an ordinary capillary. The cells typically align one behind another.
notes.D: Four cells across would require a substantially wider vessel. A typical capillary accommodates erythrocytes in single file.
notes.E: Five erythrocytes abreast are incompatible with the narrow lumen of a typical exchange capillary.

set-01-B-015.why: Initial lymphatic vessels begin as blind-ended channels in tissue. Overlapping endothelial edges can open when interstitial pressure rises, admitting fluid and macromolecules into the lymphatic network.

notes.A: Blood capillaries usually form a connected exchange network between arterioles and venules. They do not collect interstitial fluid through blind ends.
notes.B: Sinusoids are specialised wider blood channels, such as those linking inflow to central veins in the liver.
notes.C: Venules receive blood from capillaries and carry it toward veins. They are part of a continuous blood circuit.
notes.E: Coronary arteries arise from the aorta and branch toward myocardial exchange vessels. They do not begin in the interstitium.

set-01-B-016.why: Mitral stenosis obstructs flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle. It imposes a diastolic pressure gradient across the valve and slows ventricular filling.

notes.A: Aortic stenosis obstructs systolic outflow. Later ventricular hypertrophy can affect relaxation, but the valve lesion does not directly obstruct mitral inflow.
notes.B: Tricuspid regurgitation permits backward flow from the right ventricle during systole. It does not directly narrow left ventricular inflow.
notes.D: Pulmonary stenosis impedes flow from the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery. It is downstream of the tricuspid valve.
notes.E: A faster rate shortens diastole and may limit total filling time. It does not produce the direct inflow obstruction of mitral stenosis.

set-01-B-017.why: If one ventricle ejects more blood, the other receives more filling over subsequent beats. The Frank–Starling response increases stroke volume with preload and helps restore balance.

notes.A: Sympathetic input changes contractility and heart rate and can adjust overall flow. The intrinsic matching response to increased filling does not require it.
notes.B: Parasympathetic input mainly adjusts nodal activity and heart rate. It is not the intrinsic link between filling and ventricular output.
notes.C: Circulating adrenaline can increase ventricular contractility. Matching of each ventricle’s output to its own filling does not depend on an adrenaline change.
notes.E: The named intrinsic filling–output relation accounts for the matching. Autonomic and adrenal influences can modify performance but are not all required.

set-01-B-018.why: Rapid ejection starts when left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure and opens the aortic valve. Aortic inflow initially exceeds peripheral runoff, so aortic pressure rises.

notes.A: The mitral valve remains closed while left ventricular pressure exceeds left atrial pressure. It opens later when the ventricle relaxes.
notes.C: The aortic valve is open during ventricular ejection, allowing blood to enter the aorta from the ventricle.
notes.D: Ventricular volume falls during rapid and then reduced ejection. It reaches its lowest value at end-systole.
notes.E: The first heart sound begins around atrioventricular valve closure, during isovolumetric contraction before aortic ejection starts.

set-01-B-019.why: In the classical Starling model, raising interstitial protein raises its oncotic pressure and favours filtration. The revised model distinguishes bulk interstitial protein from conditions beneath the endothelial glycocalyx.

notes.A: Additional filtered fluid can raise interstitial pressure and increase lymphatic drainage while lymphatic transport capacity remains available.
notes.B: Protein raises the colloid osmotic pressure of interstitial fluid through its osmotic effect across a protein-restricting barrier.
notes.D: If lymphatic return cannot clear the extra filtered fluid, interstitial volume increases and oedema can develop.
notes.E: A rise in interstitial oncotic pressure narrows the plasma-to-interstitium difference in the classical model if plasma protein is unchanged.

set-01-B-020.why: Left ventricular electrical activation begins slightly earlier, but right ventricular ejection can start first because the pulmonary valve opens against a lower downstream arterial pressure.

notes.A: The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to generate pressure for the systemic circulation. Its muscle mass is normally greater.
notes.B: The earliest sites of ventricular activation lie on the left endocardial surface. Right ventricular activation follows shortly.
notes.C: The left ventricle generates higher pressure to drive systemic flow. The right ventricle pumps into the lower-pressure pulmonary circuit.
notes.D: With comparable stroke volumes, the higher pressure of left ventricular ejection requires more external stroke work.

set-02-A-001.why: For steady laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a rigid tube, Poiseuille resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius. Doubling diameter doubles radius.

notes.A: A one-half multiplier would fit simple inverse proportionality. Tube radius has a fourth-power effect under these assumptions.
notes.C: Widening the tube lowers resistance for the same fluid and length. A multiplier greater than one reverses that change.
notes.D: Sixteenfold is the increase for halving radius. Doubling it changes resistance by the reciprocal factor.
notes.E: Resistance depends strongly on lumen size even when tube length and fluid viscosity are held constant.

set-02-A-002.why: Korotkoff sounds weaken and usually disappear as cuff pressure falls below diastolic pressure. The artery remains open throughout the cycle, changing the pulse-induced tissue vibrations.

notes.A: Intermittent reopening under cuff compression accompanies the audible phase. The sounds fade as the artery remains open between pulses.
notes.B: Atrioventricular valve opening is a cardiac event. The sounds heard over the cuffed arm arise locally in and around the artery.
notes.C: The relevant pressure change is deflation of the cuff to the diastolic range, not a sudden fall in the person’s blood pressure.
notes.E: At the systolic threshold, the first tapping sounds appear as the artery begins to open transiently with each pulse.

set-02-A-003.why: The Fick method divides whole-body oxygen consumption by the arteriovenous oxygen content difference. The venous sample must represent mixed systemic venous return for a whole-body estimate.

notes.B: An oxygen balance uses oxygen consumption and oxygen content on the two sides. Carbon dioxide measurements are not required.
notes.C: Coronary sinus blood reflects myocardial oxygen extraction. The whole-body estimate needs systemic arterial and mixed venous oxygen contents.
notes.D: In steady circulation without a significant shunt the same net flow passes through both circuits. Separate contributions are not required.
notes.E: Sex can affect population reference values but is not a term in the oxygen mass-balance equation.

set-02-A-004.why: Acute blood loss reduces venous return and can lower arterial pressure. Reduced baroreceptor firing leads to vagal withdrawal and increased sympathetic stimulation, which raise heart rate.

notes.A: The smaller volume reduces filling and stroke volume. The rise in rate is mediated by a reflex response to reduced pressure.
notes.B: Increased vagal activity would slow sinoatrial firing. Blood loss normally reduces vagal efferent activity in the compensatory reflex.
notes.D: Compensation commonly includes sympathetic vasoconstriction in less immediately essential beds. Skeletal muscle vasodilatation does not explain the tachycardia.
notes.E: Vagal activity falls in the usual compensatory response. Sympathetic activation also accelerates firing of the sinoatrial node.

set-02-A-006.why: Most oxygen in blood is bound to haemoglobin inside erythrocytes. Only a small fraction is dissolved in plasma, which mainly carries other soluble or suspended substances.

notes.A: Many hormones circulate in plasma, either freely dissolved or bound to carrier proteins, before reaching their target tissues.
notes.B: Plasma tonicity helps maintain erythrocyte volume because water moves across the cell membrane in response to osmotic gradients.
notes.C: Chylomicrons enter the circulation after lymphatic transport from the intestine and carry dietary lipids in plasma.
notes.D: Antibodies such as immunoglobulins are plasma proteins that circulate to support immune defence after secretion by plasma cells.

set-02-A-007.why: Haematocrit is the fraction of whole-blood volume occupied by red cells. A value of 41 percent means erythrocytes occupy roughly two-fifths of the sampled blood volume.

notes.A: Haemoglobin is normally contained within red cells. Haematocrit does not measure plasma-free haemoglobin or haemolysis.
notes.B: The plasma fraction occupies most of the remainder after subtracting erythrocyte volume and the small buffy coat.
notes.D: The denominator includes plasma as well as formed elements. Haematocrit is not the fraction of blood cells that are erythrocytes.
notes.E: Plasma proteins form a dissolved component of plasma. Their concentration is separate from the red-cell volume fraction.

set-02-A-008.why: Normal cardiac excitation starts in spontaneously depolarising sinoatrial pacemaker cells. Intrinsic conduction spreads it through the heart, while autonomic nerves modify rate, conduction and contractile force.

notes.B: Gap junctions connect neighbouring myocytes and let local depolarising current pass between them.
notes.C: Pacemaker cells have spontaneous phase-four depolarisation, so their membrane potential does not remain stable between action potentials.
notes.D: Working atrial and ventricular myocytes normally have a relatively stable resting membrane potential until activated.
notes.E: The ventricular action-potential plateau prolongs the refractory period, preventing re-excitation through much of contraction.

set-02-A-009.why: Sinoatrial pacemaker cells normally reach threshold faster than other automatic cardiac cells. Their impulses activate the heart and suppress slower latent pacemakers before those cells discharge.

notes.A: Autonomic nerves modulate sinoatrial rate. Pacemaker dominance depends on intrinsic automaticity and persists in a denervated heart.
notes.B: Other conducting cells and working myocytes also generate action potentials. Latent pacemakers can discharge if sinoatrial drive is lost.
notes.D: A pacemaker cell has a changing diastolic membrane potential that drifts toward threshold, rather than a stable resting potential.
notes.E: Catecholamines can accelerate sinoatrial firing through beta-adrenergic signalling. Low catecholamine sensitivity is not why it is the usual pacemaker.

set-02-A-011.why: A physiological rise in ventricular end-diastolic volume increases initial fibre length. This augments force at a given inotropic state and typically raises the volume ejected.

notes.B: At an unchanged heart rate, a higher stroke volume tends to increase cardiac output rather than decrease it.
notes.C: The finding is greater ventricular filling. Venous pressure depends on how that increase occurred and need not fall.
notes.D: Within the physiological range, increased initial fibre length augments active force through length-dependent activation.
notes.E: Both ventricles respond to filling, which helps match their outputs over time. Increased end-diastolic volumes do not establish a left-to-right output difference.

set-02-A-012.why: Initial ventricular muscle fibre length helps determine how much force develops. Filling stretches the fibres before systole and increases their force through the Frank–Starling mechanism.

notes.B: Intercalated discs mechanically and electrically link cardiac cells. Their number is not the main beat-to-beat determinant of developed force.
notes.C: Gap junctions permit electrical coupling and coordinated activation. Changes in preload alter force without requiring an altered number of junctions.
notes.D: Sinoatrial depolarisation sets the rhythm. The force of working myocardial contraction also depends on initial fibre length.
notes.E: The His bundle conducts impulses toward the ventricles. Its length does not supply the preload-dependent force adjustment.

set-02-A-013.why: Positive inotropy means increased myocardial contractility. At a given initial fibre length and comparable loading conditions, the ventricle can develop more force or eject more effectively.

notes.A: Stroke volume can change with preload and afterload. A decrease in volume is not the definition of positive inotropy.
notes.B: Movement along a chemical gradient concerns transport or diffusion. Inotropy describes myocardial contractile strength.
notes.C: Repolarisation is the electrical recovery of pacemaker cells. It does not define a change in ventricular contractility.
notes.E: End-diastolic volume is an index of ventricular filling. Positive inotropy is defined independently of that initial filling.

set-02-A-014.why: Higher carotid sinus pressure increases baroreceptor firing. The reflex decreases sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity and raises cardiac vagal activity, producing vasodilatation and slowing the heart.

notes.A: Baroreceptor input inhibits sympathetic outflow to resistance vessels. Their smooth muscle relaxes because less adrenergic drive is present.
notes.B: Reduced vascular resistance and slower cardiac rate can lower systemic arterial pressure, including pressure in the aorta.
notes.C: Increased vagal activity slows the sinoatrial pacemaker and produces reflex bradycardia.
notes.D: Withdrawal of sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone causes arteriolar dilatation and lowers systemic vascular resistance.

set-02-A-015.why: Vagal acetylcholine activates cardiac muscarinic receptors and slows sinoatrial pacemaker depolarisation. It also slows conduction through the atrioventricular node, helping reduce the heart rate.

notes.B: Parasympathetic input decreases sinoatrial firing rather than accelerating it. Acetylcholine increases potassium conductance and reduces pacemaker cyclic AMP.
notes.C: The atrioventricular node conducts more slowly under vagal stimulation and may transmit fewer impulses if stimulation is strong.
notes.D: Vagal stimulation does not give a general increase in contractile force. It can reduce atrial contraction, with less direct ventricular effect.
notes.E: Slowing of the heart is the expected response. The listed increases in nodal activity and force do not accompany normal vagal stimulation.

set-02-A-016.why: Contracting skeletal muscle generates local signals that relax its resistance vessels. The resulting active hyperaemia increases perfusion in proportion to demand despite heightened systemic sympathetic activity.

notes.A: A higher pressure can contribute to flow, but local reduction in resistance is the main determinant of increased perfusion of active fibres.
notes.B: Alpha-adrenergic stimulation generally increases vascular smooth muscle tone. Local metabolic signals can attenuate its effect in active muscle.
notes.C: Beta-adrenergic effects can influence perfusion. Locally generated signals best explain matching of flow to the muscles actually contracting.
notes.D: Splanchnic and renal vasoconstriction can redistribute cardiac output. It does not directly lower resistance in the exercising muscle bed.

set-02-A-017.why: In many organs local blood flow adapts to metabolic activity. Increased substrate use and changes in interstitial signals relax resistance vessels and raise tissue perfusion.

notes.A: Transmural pressure can trigger a myogenic response and help stabilise flow. Metabolic control matches delivery to the tissue’s demand.
notes.C: Local transmitter release can affect vessel tone, but metabolic vasodilator signals provide a major link between cellular activity and perfusion.
notes.D: Circulating mediators can alter overall vascular tone. They do not usually provide the most precise feedback for an individual active tissue.
notes.E: Cardiac output is the total systemic flow. Local arteriolar resistance helps determine the proportion reaching a particular organ.

set-02-A-018.why: The surface electrocardiographic P wave represents summed atrial myocardial depolarisation. Small structures of the specialised conduction system ordinarily have signals too weak to appear separately.

notes.A: Sinoatrial depolarisation initiates the beat, but the small pacemaker tissue does not produce its own distinct surface deflection.
notes.B: Atrioventricular nodal conduction contributes to the PR interval. Nodal depolarisation itself is not displayed as a distinct wave.
notes.C: His-bundle signals can be measured with intracardiac electrodes. Ordinary surface ECG does not show a distinct His depolarisation wave.
notes.D: Bachmann’s bundle helps spread excitation between the atria. Its activity contributes to atrial activation without a separate visible surface wave.

set-02-A-021.why: At matched heart rate and afterload, a more contractile ventricle ejects more from the same end-diastolic volume. A higher output at comparable filling therefore supports increased inotropy.

notes.A: An end-systolic volume alone does not control for starting volume or heart rate. Comparison should begin at comparable end-diastolic filling.
notes.C: Lower output at a given residual volume does not support enhanced ejection. Initial filling and heart rate may also differ.
notes.D: At the same filling, lower output tends to indicate poorer pumping if rate and afterload are held constant.
notes.E: Ventricular refractoriness reflects action-potential timing. It does not identify an increase in contractile performance.

set-02-A-022.why: The PR interval covers atrial activation and conduction toward the ventricles before the QRS complex. The QRS, ST and QT portions all include ventricular activation or its aftermath.

notes.A: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation, with activation travelling through the ventricular myocardium.
notes.B: The QT interval runs from the onset of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave and includes depolarisation and repolarisation.
notes.C: During the ST segment most ventricular myocardium remains depolarised, with little net voltage gradient across it.

set-02-A-023.why: Raised venous pressure is transmitted upstream to capillaries, increasing the pressure that drives filtration. Oedema can develop when excess filtration exceeds the capacity for lymphatic return.

notes.A: Arteriolar constriction decreases downstream capillary pressure and usually limits the hydrostatic drive to filtration.
notes.C: An increase in plasma proteins raises intravascular oncotic pressure, which tends to oppose filtration across the microvascular barrier.
notes.D: Dehydration usually lowers vascular volume and can concentrate plasma proteins. Those changes do not generally favour hydrostatic oedema.

set-02-A-024.why: The systolic rise in cytosolic calcium activates cardiac myofilaments by binding to troponin. A greater calcium transient usually increases developed force at a given muscle length.

notes.A: Intracellular sodium influences calcium handling through the sodium–calcium exchanger. Calcium is the immediate activating ion for contraction.
notes.B: Potassium contributes to membrane potential and repolarisation. It does not directly activate cardiac myofilaments.
notes.D: Chloride contributes to some membrane currents and cell volume regulation. It is not the principal link to contractile force.
notes.E: Magnesium supports enzyme and ATP functions. It does not substitute for calcium binding to troponin during activation.

set-02-A-025.why: The pulmonary and systemic circuits operate in series. Over time right and left ventricular outputs are approximately equal, otherwise blood would accumulate in one circuit.

notes.A: With a persistent output of one-quarter of left ventricular flow, the pulmonary circuit would lose blood faster than it receives it.
notes.B: A sustained one-half ratio is incompatible with steady volumes in circuits that receive and pass on the same blood.
notes.C: A transient mismatch can occur during breathing or posture changes. It cannot be sustained at a three-quarter ratio.
notes.E: A persistent right-sided output greater than left-sided output would congest the pulmonary circuit rather than maintain steady flow.

set-02-A-026.why: Rapid cardiovascular reflexes chiefly defend arterial pressure by adjusting heart rate, cardiac contractility and vascular tone. These adjustments preserve perfusion despite changes in posture or circulating volume.

notes.A: Local metabolic control helps match oxygen delivery to tissue need. The arterial baroreflex directly senses vessel stretch related to pressure.
notes.B: Resistance can vary widely because arterioles are effectors of cardiovascular reflexes rather than a fixed target.
notes.D: Cardiac output changes with demand and contributes to regulation. Reflex regulation does not require that output stay constant.

set-02-A-027.why: Slow conduction through the atrioventricular node delays ventricular activation after the atria depolarise. This gives atrial contraction time to finish contributing to ventricular filling.

notes.A: Aortic runoff is driven by the arterial pressure gradient during diastole. It is not the primary purpose of the nodal delay.
notes.B: Systemic and pulmonary venous return reach the atria during much of the cycle. The delay specifically allows atria to empty into ventricles.
notes.D: Ventricular contraction follows transmission of the impulse beyond the node. The delay postpones contraction so filling can finish first.
notes.E: Ventricular repolarisation occurs after ventricular activation, well after the atrioventricular delay has ended.

set-02-A-028.why: Preload reflects ventricular muscle stretch before contraction. Left ventricular end-diastolic volume is a useful estimate because it reflects chamber filling more directly than upstream pressure measurements.

notes.A: Total blood volume influences venous return but does not specify the volume or stretch in a particular ventricle.
notes.B: Central venous pressure is a right-sided filling pressure. It does not directly measure left ventricular end-diastolic size.
notes.C: Wedge pressure approximates left atrial pressure in appropriate circumstances. It does not directly measure ventricular volume or fibre stretch.
notes.E: End-diastolic pressure depends on compliance as well as filling. The same pressure can occur at different ventricular volumes.

set-02-A-029.why: Inspiration increases right-sided venous return and can prolong right ventricular ejection. The pulmonary valve closes later, widening the physiological separation between the two components of the second sound.

notes.A: Inspiration may make aortic closure slightly earlier as left ventricular filling falls. Delayed aortic closure would tend to narrow the split.
notes.B: Opening of the mitral valve begins ventricular filling. It does not produce either normal semilunar closure component of the second sound.
notes.D: Right ventricular filling rises during inspiration, while left ventricular filling can fall transiently. A rise in left stroke volume is not the main mechanism.
notes.E: Heart rate may change with breathing, but the split reflects the relative timing of aortic and pulmonary valve closure.

set-02-A-030.why: Anaemia reduces the oxygen carried in each unit of blood. Lower viscosity and compensatory changes in vascular resistance and cardiac flow can produce a sustained high-output state.

notes.A: Hypertension is elevated pressure and often reflects increased vascular resistance. It does not by itself imply sustained high output.
notes.B: Aortic stenosis obstructs left ventricular ejection and can limit increases in output, especially during exercise.
notes.D: Complete heart block can leave a slow ventricular escape rhythm. The reduced rate often limits cardiac output.
notes.E: Cardiac tamponade limits diastolic filling, reducing stroke volume and usually lowering cardiac output.

set-02-A-031.why: Markedly raised intracranial pressure can evoke the Cushing response. Sympathetic vasoconstriction raises arterial pressure to defend cerebral perfusion, and the arterial pressure rise can trigger reflex bradycardia.

notes.A: Dynamic exercise typically raises systolic pressure and heart rate together. A fall in rate is not the usual exertional response.
notes.B: Increased body temperature often produces tachycardia and increased skin flow. It does not characteristically cause hypertension with reflex bradycardia.
notes.C: Acute altitude exposure often increases sympathetic drive and heart rate as oxygen availability falls.
notes.E: Haemorrhage reduces circulating volume and usually causes tachycardia as arterial pressure or filling falls.

set-02-A-032.why: Increased resistance downstream of capillaries raises pressure upstream within them. The higher capillary hydrostatic pressure increases the outward driving force for fluid filtration.

notes.A: Precapillary constriction reduces pressure in the capillary bed supplied by that vessel and generally reduces filtration there.
notes.B: Lower arterial pressure generally decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure unless compensatory changes maintain it.
notes.C: More plasma protein raises intravascular oncotic pressure and strengthens the opposing effect on outward filtration.
notes.D: Reduced hydraulic permeability lowers fluid movement for a given driving pressure. It does not by itself increase filtration.

set-02-A-033.why: Systemic venules and veins hold the largest fraction of blood volume at rest. Their high compliance allows considerable storage at low pressure and supports redistribution when demand changes.

notes.A: The cardiac chambers contain blood during filling and ejection. Their combined volume is much smaller than the systemic venous reservoir.
notes.B: The aorta carries high pressure and supplies major arteries. Its lumen stores only a small fraction of total blood volume.
notes.C: Arteries and arterioles distribute blood and regulate resistance. They are less compliant and contain less blood than systemic veins.
notes.D: Capillaries provide a vast exchange area. Their small luminal volumes add up to less than the venous compartment.

set-02-A-034.why: Higher flow velocity increases the Reynolds number, favouring turbulence. For a given geometry, the Reynolds number rises when inertial forces increase relative to viscous damping.

notes.B: Higher viscosity damps disturbances and lowers Reynolds number, making turbulence less likely if other variables are unchanged.
notes.C: At fixed velocity, a smaller diameter lowers Reynolds number. A real stenosis can raise local velocity, so its effects interact.
notes.D: Lower density decreases fluid inertia at a given velocity and diameter and therefore decreases Reynolds number.
notes.E: Length increases resistance in a straight tube, but it is not a term in the standard Reynolds number relation.

set-02-A-036.why: Flow in many peripheral veins is relatively smooth because upstream resistance dampens arterial pulsations. Venous flow can still vary with breathing, muscle contraction and proximity to the heart.

notes.A: Central venous flow can be phasic, but prominent pressure waves from ventricular ejection are characteristic of arteries.
notes.C: Most systemic veins return relatively deoxygenated blood toward the heart. They do not deliver oxygen directly to systemic capillaries.
notes.D: Velocity depends on flow and total cross-sectional area. Veins are not generally faster than corresponding arteries.
notes.E: Pressure gradients and valves normally support net flow toward the heart. Sustained bidirectional flow is not the usual pattern.

set-02-A-037.why: Pulmonary and systemic circuits are connected in series, so their net flows are closely matched in steady state. Pulmonary vascular resistance is substantially lower than systemic resistance.

notes.B: The pulmonary circuit carries comparable flow at a much lower pressure difference, implying lower vascular resistance.
notes.C: Pulmonary venous blood has given up carbon dioxide in the lungs. It normally contains less carbon dioxide than pulmonary arterial blood.
notes.D: Pulmonary hypertension increases pressure load on the right ventricle and can cause right ventricular hypertrophy.
notes.E: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood into the left atrium. Systemic veins supply blood to the right atrium.

set-02-A-041.why: Resting working myocardial cells are most permeable to potassium, so membrane potential lies near the potassium equilibrium potential. Other ion permeabilities and the sodium–potassium pump help sustain it.

notes.A: Sodium permeability rises when fast sodium channels open during ventricular depolarisation. Resting sodium conductance is comparatively low.
notes.C: Calcium channels contribute to the action-potential plateau and contraction. Resting potential mainly reflects potassium conductance.
notes.D: Chloride currents can affect electrical behaviour, but they do not normally dominate the resting potential of contractile myocytes.
notes.E: The sodium–potassium pump maintains the gradients and has a small electrogenic effect. Resting potassium permeability is the immediate determinant.

set-03-A-001.why: The sinoatrial node usually reaches firing threshold before the heart’s other automatic tissues. Its impulses activate the atria and entrain slower pacemakers during normal sinus rhythm.

notes.B: The atrioventricular node conducts atrial impulses and can generate a slower escape rhythm if sinoatrial drive fails.
notes.C: The His bundle conducts impulses to ventricular branches. Its latent automaticity does not normally set heart rate.
notes.D: The mitral valve is a mechanical structure regulating flow. It does not generate the normal pacemaker impulse.
notes.E: Ventricular escape rhythms can occur when higher pacemakers fail. Normal impulses originate before they reach the ventricles.

set-03-A-002.why: The QRS complex is the surface ECG expression of ventricular myocardial depolarisation. Atrial repolarisation usually occurs around the same time but is obscured by the larger signal.

notes.A: Atrial depolarisation generates the P wave, which ordinarily precedes the QRS complex.
notes.B: Atrial repolarisation may overlap the QRS complex in time. Ventricular activation is the dominant source of that complex.
notes.D: Ventricular repolarisation is represented mainly by the T wave, which follows the QRS complex.
notes.E: Atrioventricular conduction delay contributes to the PR interval and occurs before the ventricles produce the QRS complex.

set-03-A-003.why: An ECG can show whether atrial electrical activity reaches the ventricles. Comparing P waves with QRS complexes and assessing the PR interval helps identify atrioventricular conduction abnormalities.

notes.A: A murmur is a mechanical sound usually detected by auscultation. An ECG does not directly record heart sounds.
notes.B: Stroke volume is blood volume ejected per beat. It requires a haemodynamic or imaging measurement rather than electrical timing alone.
notes.C: An ECG can provide heart rate, but calculating cardiac output also requires stroke volume or an independent flow measurement.
notes.E: Atrioventricular conduction can be assessed from timing and relationships on an ECG, so a relevant use is listed.

set-03-A-004.why: Cardiac output is the amount ejected by one ventricle per minute and equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. In steady state it approximates systemic blood flow.

notes.A: Either ventricular output can represent cardiac output in a steady circulation. The outputs are measured separately rather than added.
notes.B: Systemic flow per minute is what the left ventricle supplies in steady state, so this is another expression of cardiac output.
notes.C: Multiplying beats per minute by volume per beat gives volume per minute, the units of cardiac output.
notes.D: Ventricular flow and the rate–stroke volume relation are valid. The selection omits the equivalent steady-state systemic flow description.

set-03-A-005.why: Increased venous return raises ventricular filling and stretches myocardial fibres. Within physiological limits, the resulting increase in force raises stroke volume through the Frank–Starling mechanism.

notes.A: Both ventricles generally eject comparable volumes over time. The mechanism helps match output to filling rather than giving the left ventricle a persistent excess.
notes.B: Intrinsic pacemaker rate is a property of automatic cells. The Starling mechanism concerns ventricular filling and ejection.
notes.C: Heart rate is a factor in cardiac output. The specific Starling response links initial fibre length to stroke volume.
notes.E: The timing of ventricular contraction reflects the conduction system. The Starling relation addresses mechanical force and output.

set-03-A-006.why: Protodiastole refers to the short transition from late ejection to semilunar valve closure as ventricular pressure falls. Atrioventricular valves remain closed until ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.

notes.A: Open atrioventricular valves indicate the subsequent filling phase. They remain shut at the end of ventricular ejection.
notes.B: Both sets are closed during isovolumetric relaxation after semilunar closure. Protodiastole includes the transition toward that closure.
notes.C: Atrioventricular valves are closed before ejection ends. The semilunar valves are moving toward closure rather than both sets remaining open.
notes.E: There is a valid description in which the semilunar valves close while atrioventricular valves are still closed.

set-03-A-008.why: Isovolumetric contraction starts after atrioventricular valves close and ends when semilunar valves open. Both sets are closed between those events, so ventricular pressure rises at constant volume.

notes.A: Open inflow and outflow valves would allow chamber volume to change. Neither set is open during normal isovolumetric contraction.
notes.B: Closed atrioventricular valves with open semilunar valves indicate ejection, when ventricular volume decreases.
notes.C: Open atrioventricular valves with closed semilunar valves characterise ventricular filling, when the ventricles gain volume.
notes.E: Both sets are closed during the pressure rise before ejection. That configuration is represented among the choices.

set-03-A-009.why: The aortic valve closes when left ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure at the end of ejection. Its closed leaflets prevent aortic blood returning to the ventricle.

notes.A: During diastole the higher pressure is in the aorta. The valve prevents flow out of the aorta back toward the ventricle.
notes.C: During forward ejection the valve is open and ventricular pressure drives flow into the aorta. The backflow-preventing closure occurs later.
notes.D: Ejection is forward flow into the aorta. The valve does not block that normal direction when the ventricle is ejecting.
notes.E: Aortic valve closure supplies one component of the second sound. The first sound is associated with atrioventricular valve closure.

set-03-A-011.why: Heart sounds are mechanical vibrations associated with cardiac events such as valve closure. A stethoscope allows auscultation, while phonocardiography records the acoustic signal for analysis.

notes.A: Arterial wall fluctuations produce the arterial pulse and can be timed alongside heart sounds. They are not the cardiac sounds themselves.
notes.B: Bioelectrical activity is recorded by electrocardiography. Heart sounds reflect mechanical vibration during the cardiac cycle.
notes.C: Blood flow per minute defines cardiac output and requires a flow estimate. Acoustic timing alone does not measure it.
notes.E: Phlebography evaluates veins or, in older terminology, venous pulsations. Heart sound waveforms are recorded by phonocardiography.

set-03-A-012.why: At rest the kidneys receive a large fraction of cardiac output relative to their small mass. This produces the highest perfusion per 100 grams among the listed tissues.

notes.A: The brain has continuous perfusion to support metabolism. Its resting flow per 100 grams is substantially below renal perfusion.
notes.B: The myocardium has high oxygen extraction and a rich blood supply. Resting flow per mass is still below that of the kidneys.
notes.C: Skin flow varies with temperature and autonomic tone. Typical resting perfusion per 100 grams is lower than renal perfusion.
notes.D: The liver receives substantial total blood flow through two routes. Dividing this by its larger mass gives lower flow per 100 grams.

set-03-A-013.why: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Seventy beats per minute times 75 millilitres per beat gives 5,250 millilitres, or 5.25 litres, per minute.

notes.A: The specified heart rate and stroke volume yield more than this. Multiplying them gives 5,250 millilitres per minute.
notes.B: A flow of 4.55 litres per minute at 70 beats per minute would require a smaller stroke volume of 65 millilitres.
notes.D: A cardiac output of eight litres per minute would require more than 110 millilitres per beat at the given rate.
notes.E: Nearly ten litres per minute would require about 140 millilitres per beat at 70 beats per minute, above the given volume.

set-03-A-014.why: The QRS complex reflects rapid depolarisation of ventricular myocardium. The impulse spreads through the His–Purkinje system and then through ventricular muscle, generating the recorded deflection.

notes.A: The PQ or PR interval extends from the start of atrial depolarisation to the start of ventricular activation.
notes.C: The QT interval includes ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation. The QRS complex is the component representing activation alone.
notes.D: The ST segment follows the QRS and corresponds to a period when much of the ventricular myocardium is already depolarised.
notes.E: The T wave is the principal surface expression of ventricular repolarisation after the QRS complex.

set-03-A-015.why: The right and left ventricles supply two circulations connected in series. Their mean outputs are approximately equal in steady state, although small transient differences can occur.

notes.A: A sustained right output of only one-quarter of left output would quickly deplete the pulmonary vascular compartment.
notes.B: One-half would represent an ongoing imbalance, causing blood to accumulate on the systemic side rather than circulate steadily.
notes.C: Brief beat-to-beat mismatches can occur with breathing. A persistent three-quarter ratio is incompatible with stable circuit volumes.
notes.E: A prolonged excess of right over left output would raise pulmonary blood volume rather than maintain steady state.

set-03-A-016.why: Ventricular filling occurs when atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure and opens the atrioventricular valves. The semilunar valves remain closed because arterial pressure exceeds relaxing ventricular pressure.

notes.A: Open semilunar valves would connect the ventricles to the arteries. The outflow valves remain closed during normal filling.
notes.B: Closed atrioventricular valves and open semilunar valves characterise ventricular ejection, which decreases ventricular volume.
notes.D: Both sets are closed during isovolumetric phases. Ventricular volume is then constant because no inflow valve is open.
notes.E: The normal filling configuration is represented among the options. Inflow valves are open and outflow valves are closed.

set-03-A-017.why: Cardiac sympathetic stimulation increases contractile force and speeds conduction, especially through the atrioventricular node. The rise in cardiac work also increases myocardial energy and oxygen demand.

notes.A: Beta-1 stimulation increases intracellular calcium availability and can strengthen myocardial contraction at a given initial length.
notes.B: A faster, more forceful heart performs more work and consumes more oxygen. Cardiac metabolic demand therefore rises.
notes.C: Sympathetic stimulation increases atrioventricular nodal conduction velocity, shortening the delay between atrial and ventricular activation.
notes.D: The usual cardiac adrenergic response does not decrease excitability. It increases pacemaker activity and can facilitate conduction.

set-03-A-018.why: Ventricular myocytes have a long action potential with a plateau sustained in part by inward calcium current. The plateau lengthens refractoriness and prevents summation of contractions.

notes.A: Skeletal muscle action potentials last only a few milliseconds. Ventricular myocyte repolarisation is delayed by the plateau.
notes.B: Ventricular cells have a strongly negative resting potential. Their normal phase-zero upstroke is rapid, rather than a slow drift from zero.
notes.C: The ventricular upstroke is driven mainly by fast sodium influx. Calcium contributes strongly to the later plateau and to nodal upstrokes.
notes.E: Ventricular myocardium has a long refractory period. This limits re-excitation and prevents normal tetanic summation.

set-03-A-020.why: Heart rate counts cycles per minute, so cycle duration is its reciprocal after conversion to seconds. A faster rate shortens the cycle, reducing diastole especially.

notes.A: Stroke volume measures blood ejected per beat. It does not directly set the time between successive beats.
notes.B: Systole is only part of the cycle. The time from one beat to the next also includes diastole.
notes.C: Diastole is the filling and relaxation portion. Total cycle duration includes both ventricular relaxation and contraction.
notes.E: The cardiac pause describes a period within the cycle. Beat frequency determines the time available for the complete cycle.

set-03-A-021.why: Hypokalaemia alters ventricular repolarisation and can produce prominent U waves following flattened T waves. The U wave can merge with the T wave and distort interval measurement.

notes.A: A shortened PR interval is not characteristic. Significant hypokalaemia can slow conduction and sometimes prolong PR.
notes.C: ST depression is more typical than ST elevation in hypokalaemia, often alongside T-wave flattening.
notes.D: Tall, narrow, peaked T waves suggest hyperkalaemia. A flatter T wave and prominent U wave favour hypokalaemia.
notes.E: T and U waves can merge, giving apparent QT or QU prolongation. A shortened QT is not the typical finding here.

set-03-A-022.why: An early recognised ECG effect of hyperkalaemia is a narrow, peaked T wave caused by altered ventricular repolarisation. ECG findings vary and may be absent despite elevated potassium.

notes.B: Prominent U waves more strongly suggest hypokalaemia, particularly when the preceding T waves are flattened.
notes.C: Early hyperkalaemia can shorten ventricular repolarisation. With more severe toxicity, conduction abnormalities such as QRS widening become prominent.
notes.D: ST depression and flattened T waves are more typical of low potassium in this comparison.
notes.E: More advanced hyperkalaemia can prolong the PR interval and attenuate P waves. A shortened PR is not the characteristic early change.

set-03-A-023.why: Left ventricular end-diastolic volume is the amount of blood present just before systole. A value around 100 to 130 millilitres is a common adult teaching estimate.

notes.A: A total end-diastolic volume of 10 to 30 millilitres is much lower than typical adult filling values.
notes.B: Thirty to fifty millilitres is closer to the residual amount that can remain at end-systole in many adults.
notes.C: Fifty to seventy millilitres is a common range for stroke volume, which is the amount ejected rather than the whole filled chamber volume.
notes.D: Smaller adults can have volumes within this range. The conventional unindexed teaching example of a filled ventricle is nearer 120 millilitres.

set-03-A-024.why: Distal His–Purkinje tissue can generate a slow ventricular escape rhythm when higher pacemakers fail. Intrinsic rates of about 20 to 40 impulses per minute are taught for Purkinje cells.

notes.A: Proximal His tissue is part of the atrioventricular junctional system. Its typical escape rate is higher than the distal ventricular range.
notes.B: The atrioventricular junctional escape rate is usually around 40 to 60 impulses per minute.
notes.C: The sinoatrial node has the highest normal intrinsic firing rate and usually dominates the slower distal pacemakers.
notes.E: The bundle branches mainly distribute the impulse. A slow distal automatic rate is classically assigned to the Purkinje network.

set-03-A-026.why: Atrial natriuretic peptide is released when the atria stretch. It promotes renal sodium excretion and can relax vascular smooth muscle, helping counter increased circulating volume.

notes.A: Noradrenaline stimulates alpha-adrenergic receptors on many resistance vessels, producing vasoconstriction in those beds.
notes.B: Vasopressin can constrict vessels through vascular V1 receptors, in addition to its renal water-conserving action.
notes.C: Serotonin can constrict certain vessels, including through smooth muscle serotonin receptors. The effect can vary by vascular bed and endothelium.
notes.D: Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that acts on vascular smooth muscle and helps raise arterial pressure.

set-03-A-027.why: Conduction is slowest in the atrioventricular node. Its cellular properties create a delay between atrial and ventricular activation, leaving time for atrial emptying before ventricular contraction.

notes.A: Activation passes from the sinoatrial region through atrial myocardium faster than through the atrioventricular node.
notes.C: The His bundle rapidly carries excitation from the atrioventricular junction toward the bundle branches.
notes.D: Purkinje fibres have particularly fast conduction, helping activate widely separated regions of the ventricles nearly together.
notes.E: Working ventricular muscle conducts more slowly than Purkinje fibres, but the specialised atrioventricular node supplies the principal slow segment.

set-03-A-028.why: Adrenaline activates alpha and beta adrenergic receptors, including alpha-1, beta-1 and beta-2. Its relative cardiovascular effects depend on concentration and the receptor populations present.

notes.A: Noradrenaline has strong alpha and beta-1 activity but comparatively weak beta-2 activity, so it lacks the same broad profile.
notes.C: Isoprenaline strongly activates beta-1 and beta-2 receptors. It has little alpha-1 activity.
notes.D: Phenylephrine primarily activates alpha-1 receptors and increases vascular tone. It is not a strong beta agonist.
notes.E: Dobutamine acts predominantly through beta-1 receptors, with additional effects that do not match adrenaline’s broad profile.

set-03-A-029.why: A narrowed mitral valve obstructs left atrial emptying during diastole. The resulting low-pitched diastolic rumble is usually heard best at the cardiac apex.

notes.A: A continuous murmur extends across systole and diastole. Flow across the narrowed mitral valve occurs chiefly during ventricular filling.
notes.B: A systolic murmur at the base suggests an outflow lesion such as aortic stenosis. Mitral inflow is diastolic.
notes.D: A diastolic murmur at the base may reflect semilunar regurgitation. Mitral stenosis is usually best heard at the apex.
notes.E: A systolic apical murmur suggests mitral regurgitation. Stenosis produces noise during forward diastolic inflow.

set-03-A-030.why: Peripheral chemoreceptors increase their firing when arterial oxygen tension falls. Carotid bodies also respond to raised carbon dioxide and acidity, stimulating ventilation when gas exchange is inadequate.

notes.A: Higher arterial pressure activates baroreceptors. It is not the usual direct chemical stimulus to peripheral chemoreceptors.
notes.C: Lower arterial carbon dioxide generally reduces chemical drive. Increased carbon dioxide instead stimulates peripheral chemoreceptor activity.
notes.D: A decrease in hydrogen ion concentration means lower acidity. Increased acidity stimulates carotid-body activity.
notes.E: Cooling changes metabolism and ventilation, but low arterial oxygen tension is the direct chemoreceptor stimulus specified here.

set-03-A-031.why: Resting myocardium has a high continuous requirement for aerobic ATP production. Per 100 grams it typically consumes more oxygen than the other listed tissues under resting conditions.

notes.A: The brain has a large total oxygen requirement. Per unit mass, resting myocardium generally consumes more oxygen.
notes.C: The liver has a substantial total metabolic demand. Much of that total reflects its larger organ mass.
notes.D: Kidneys receive high blood flow, but oxygen extraction is comparatively low. High perfusion does not equate to the highest consumption per mass.
notes.E: Resting skeletal muscle uses relatively little oxygen per unit mass. Consumption increases substantially during contraction.

set-03-A-032.why: The lower systolic pressure of the right ventricle causes less intramyocardial vascular compression. Right coronary inflow supplying the right ventricle therefore persists through more of systole.

notes.A: Anatomical dominance depends on the origin of the posterior descending artery. Right dominance is more common than left dominance.
notes.B: Left ventricular contraction compresses intramural vessels, especially subendocardially. Left coronary flow commonly falls during systole.
notes.D: Diastole is the main period of perfusion of left ventricular muscle because systolic compression has subsided.
notes.E: Right ventricular systolic compression is less intense. Right coronary flow to that region can continue during systole.

set-03-A-035.why: Isovolumetric contraction is the early pressure-building part of ventricular systole. Both inflow and outflow valves are closed, so ventricular volume cannot fall until ejection begins.

notes.A: Ejection starts when ventricular pressure opens the semilunar valves. The preceding pressure-building phase has no outflow.
notes.C: Ventricular diastole includes relaxation and filling. Isovolumetric contraction belongs to the start of systole.
notes.D: Rapid filling requires open atrioventricular valves and falling ventricular pressure. Neither condition describes early systolic contraction.
notes.E: Slow filling occurs later in diastole before atrial contraction. Ventricular pressure generation with closed valves is a separate phase.

set-03-A-037.why: Asynchronous contraction is the early part of ventricular systole, when different ventricular regions develop tension as activation spreads. Coordinated pressure rise then leads into isovolumetric contraction.

notes.B: The ventricles are beginning to contract, so this is an early systolic event rather than a filling or relaxation phase.
notes.C: Semilunar closure occurs at the end of ejection and begins isovolumetric relaxation, much later than initial activation.
notes.D: By semilunar opening the ventricles have already completed isovolumetric pressure development and are ready to eject.
notes.E: Atrioventricular opening marks the start of filling in diastole. Early ventricular contraction occurs later.

set-03-A-038.why: Standard bipolar limb leads I, II and III each record a voltage difference between two limb electrodes. Their orientations view the heart in the frontal plane.

notes.A: The augmented limb leads use a limb electrode compared with a composite reference, so they are conventionally called unipolar leads.
notes.C: The precordial leads use chest electrodes and a composite reference. They view activation mainly in the horizontal plane.
notes.D: The standard limb combination is valid. Adding the augmented leads would include recordings outside the standard bipolar set.
notes.E: Neither the augmented limb leads nor the precordial leads form the standard bipolar limb group.

set-03-A-040.why: Arterial baroreceptors adjust autonomic output in both directions. Falling pressure evokes a pressor response, while rising pressure evokes a depressor response that buffers the change.

notes.B: Reduced baroreceptor firing favours a pressor response. Increased firing activates the opposite reflex direction.
notes.C: The arterial baroreflex is especially important for rapid pressure buffering. Sustained regulation also involves renal and endocrine mechanisms.
notes.D: Increased firing produces a depressor response, but falling firing can increase sympathetic tone and evoke a pressor response.
notes.E: The Bainbridge response is associated with atrial stretch during increased venous return. The arterial pressure reflex uses separate receptors.

set-03-A-041.why: Cardiac sympathetic fibres directly accelerate the sinoatrial pacemaker. Noradrenaline stimulates beta-1 receptors, increasing the rate at which pacemaker cells reach threshold between beats.

notes.B: Parasympathetic stimulation releases acetylcholine and usually slows the sinoatrial node through muscarinic signalling.
notes.C: A fall in pressure can raise heart rate through the baroreflex. The direct cardiac effector is altered autonomic input.
notes.D: Lower pressure acts indirectly through a reflex, and increased vagal stimulation tends to slow rather than accelerate the heart.
notes.E: Sympathetic input has a direct positive chronotropic effect and is included among the choices.

set-03-A-042.why: Longer-term arterial pressure control depends strongly on renal sodium and water balance and on hormonal signals such as the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. These alter extracellular and circulating volume.

notes.A: Neural reflexes rapidly buffer changes in pressure, but durable regulation also requires adjustment of fluid and sodium balance.
notes.B: Arterial baroreflexes can reset during sustained pressure changes. They mainly supply rapid pressor and depressor buffering.
notes.D: Chemoreceptor reflexes respond to changes in gases and acidity. They do not provide the main long-term blood-volume correction.
notes.E: The hypothalamus participates in autonomic and fluid regulation. The principal long-term mechanism here includes renal and hormonal volume control.

set-03-A-043.why: The sinoatrial node generates spontaneous impulses faster than other cardiac pacemaker tissues under ordinary conditions. Its impulses initiate normal sinus rhythm and entrain downstream conducting cells.

notes.A: The atrioventricular node conducts impulses from atria to ventricles and can contribute to a slower junctional escape rhythm.
notes.B: Purkinje fibres distribute excitation in the ventricles. Their intrinsic escape rate is usually much slower than sinoatrial firing.
notes.C: The atrioventricular bundle conducts impulses into the ventricular conduction system and is ordinarily activated by the upstream pacemaker.
notes.E: The sinoatrial node is explicitly listed and normally initiates the heart’s rhythm.

set-03-A-044.why: The T wave reflects ventricular repolarisation. Differences in the timing of electrical recovery across the ventricular wall generate a measurable signal after the ST segment.

notes.A: Resting membrane potential is a cellular electrical state. The T wave is generated by changes during ventricular recovery.
notes.B: The P wave represents atrial depolarisation. It occurs before the ventricular QRS complex and T wave.
notes.C: Sinoatrial excitation initiates the beat, but its small signal is not separately identifiable on the routine surface ECG.
notes.E: Purkinje activation helps produce rapid ventricular excitation before the T wave. The T wave reflects recovery of ventricular myocardium.

set-03-A-045.why: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume. Dividing 70 millilitres by 0.55 gives approximately 127 millilitres, closest to 130 millilitres.

notes.A: An end-diastolic volume of 50 millilitres cannot supply a stroke volume of 70 millilitres from that chamber.
notes.B: If 70 millilitres were both the filling volume and the ejected volume, the ejection fraction would be 100 percent.
notes.C: A 100-millilitre end-diastolic volume and 70-millilitre stroke volume would give an ejection fraction of 70 percent.
notes.E: With a 200-millilitre filling volume and a 70-millilitre stroke volume, the ejection fraction would be 35 percent.

set-03-A-046.why: Greater vagal tone slows spontaneous depolarisation of sinoatrial nodal cells via muscarinic receptors. The longer interval between beats produces bradycardia and may also slow atrioventricular conduction.

notes.A: A slower rate can lower cardiac output if stroke volume is unchanged. Hypertension is not a direct effect of cardiac vagal stimulation.
notes.B: Tachycardia is an increase in heart rate. Vagal acetylcholine generally produces the opposite pacemaker response.
notes.D: Slowing of heart rate can lower output unless stroke volume changes sufficiently to compensate.
notes.E: A longer filling time could influence stroke volume indirectly. The characteristic direct effect is slowing of pacemaker discharge.

set-03-A-047.why: The dicrotic notch appears near aortic valve closure at the end of ventricular ejection. Brief reversal of flow and elastic recoil produce a notch on the aortic pressure trace.

notes.A: Mitral closure occurs before ejection and contributes to the first heart sound. The notch follows ejection.
notes.B: Tricuspid closure is an early systolic event on the right. It does not generate the systemic arterial notch.
notes.D: Pulmonary valve closure relates to events in the pulmonary artery. The aortic notch reflects the left ventricular outflow valve.
notes.E: Atrioventricular opening occurs after isovolumetric relaxation begins. The aortic valve has already closed at the notch.

set-03-A-048.why: Vessel radius has a large effect on regional vascular resistance. Under a simple laminar-flow model resistance varies with the inverse fourth power of radius, making arteriolar tone important.

notes.A: Higher viscosity increases resistance linearly in the ideal laminar-flow relationship. Radius has a fourth-power effect.
notes.B: Resistance increases with vessel length. Acute regional control mostly changes calibre rather than vessel length.
notes.C: Laminar flow is an assumption used to describe the radius–resistance relation. It is not the geometric variable the region adjusts.
notes.E: Venous valves help prevent backflow. Most rapid regional resistance changes result from altered arteriolar calibre.

set-03-A-050.why: A typical resting adult sinus rate lies near 60 to 90 beats per minute. Clinical reference ranges can extend to 100, and trained individuals can have lower resting rates.

notes.A: Rates well above 100 beats per minute in a resting adult represent tachycardia unless the clinical context changes the interpretation.
notes.B: Forty to sixty is often quoted as the intrinsic junctional escape range. It can also occur with low resting sinus rates in trained adults.
notes.C: A resting rate around 50 can be physiological in some individuals. It is below the usual range intended by this question.
notes.E: Twenty to forty is more typical of a distal ventricular escape pacemaker than normal resting sinus rhythm.

set-03-A-051.why: A premature ventricular beat often leaves the sinus-node timing unchanged. The next conducted beat then occurs on the original sinus schedule, producing a full compensatory pause.

notes.A: A premature atrial impulse commonly reaches and resets the sinoatrial node. The resulting pause is usually incomplete.
notes.B: Premature ventricular and atrial beats often differ in whether sinus timing is reset, so a full pause is not typical of both.
notes.D: Atrial fibrillation has irregular ventricular timing. It does not normally provide the stable sinus cycle needed to identify a classical full pause.
notes.E: Flutter timing and atrioventricular conduction can vary. The standard full compensatory pause is described relative to sinus rhythm.

set-03-A-053.why: Under normal conditions, the sinoatrial node discharges before other latent pacemakers and determines heart rhythm. A slower escape focus can take over if sinus impulses fail.

notes.A: The His bundle transmits impulses to the bundle branches. It is ordinarily activated by the upstream sinus impulse.
notes.B: The atrioventricular node influences conduction delay and can contribute to escape rhythm. It does not normally set sinus rhythm.
notes.D: Purkinje fibres rapidly carry ventricular impulses and can generate slow escape activity if higher pacemakers fail.
notes.E: The bundle branches distribute activation to the ventricles. In normal rhythm they follow the impulse initiated in the atria.

set-03-A-054.why: Tachycardia is a heart rate above the expected range for the setting, conventionally above 100 beats per minute in a resting adult. Its mechanism can vary.

notes.A: Tachypnoea means an increased respiratory rate. It concerns breathing rather than heart rate.
notes.B: Bradycardia refers to a low heart rate, which is the reverse of the finding asked about.
notes.C: Atrial fibrillation is a particular rhythm with disorganised atrial activity. Its ventricular rate can be fast, normal or slow.
notes.D: Atrial flutter is a specific atrial tachyarrhythmia. The general term for a fast heart rate does not specify that rhythm.

set-03-A-055.why: A junctional escape rhythm commonly runs at about 40 to 60 beats per minute. The atrioventricular junction takes over when faster impulses from the sinoatrial node stop reaching it.

notes.A: This range is typical of resting sinus rhythm. A junctional escape focus normally fires more slowly.
notes.B: Twenty to forty beats per minute is more typical of a distal ventricular escape rhythm.
notes.C: A junctional rhythm around 75 may be accelerated. It exceeds the classic range for a passive junctional escape.
notes.E: This wide range mixes several possible rates. A usual junctional escape is confined to a much narrower interval.

set-03-A-056.why: Automaticity is spontaneous electrical activity without an external stimulus. It occurs in cardiac pacemaker tissue and also in some spontaneously active neurons and smooth muscle cells.

notes.A: Cardiac conducting cells can fire spontaneously, but automaticity also occurs in some neuronal and smooth muscle populations.
notes.B: Typical skeletal muscle fibres require motor neuron activation. Striation does not establish whether a tissue fires spontaneously.
notes.D: Excitability is the ability to respond to a stimulus. Only some excitable cells can initiate impulses spontaneously.
notes.E: Some smooth muscle is spontaneously active, but cardiac pacemaker cells and certain neurons also show automaticity.

set-03-A-057.why: Working myocardial cells have a rapid sodium-dependent upstroke followed by a plateau and delayed repolarisation. This long action potential differs from the shorter one in skeletal muscle.

notes.A: A slow upstroke can occur in nodal cells. Working ventricular cells depolarise rapidly and have a prolonged action potential.
notes.C: The ventricular upstroke is rapid, but the plateau makes the total repolarisation process prolonged compared with skeletal muscle.
notes.D: A slow initial upstroke is not typical of working atrial or ventricular myocardium, which has fast sodium channels.
notes.E: Slow waves plus superimposed spikes describe some smooth muscle activity. Working cardiomyocytes have a distinct plateau potential.

set-03-A-058.why: The P wave represents depolarisation spreading through right and left atrial muscle. It occurs before ventricular activation, which produces the QRS complex.

notes.A: Atrial repolarisation occurs later and is usually obscured by the much larger QRS complex.
notes.B: Ventricular depolarisation generates the QRS complex. The preceding P wave comes from atrial activation.
notes.D: The P wave reflects activation, when atrial membrane potentials become less negative. It does not represent hyperpolarisation.
notes.E: The interval up to ventricular activation includes atrioventricular and conducting-system transit. The P wave itself covers atrial depolarisation.

set-03-A-059.why: Asynchronous ventricular contraction occurs at the start of systole as activation spreads through the ventricular muscle. Inflow and outflow valve transitions occur during later pressure changes.
