notes.B: Ventricular diastole consists of relaxation and filling. Asynchronous contraction is part of early active systole.
notes.C: Semilunar valves close at the end of ejection, and isovolumetric relaxation begins with both sets of valves closed.
notes.D: Opening of semilunar valves starts ventricular ejection. Initial contraction and pressure development precede it.
notes.E: Atrioventricular valves open when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure. This occurs in diastole before the next contraction.

set-03-A-060.why: In complete atrioventricular block, atrial impulses fail to conduct to the ventricles. The atria follow their own rhythm while a junctional or ventricular escape focus produces independent QRS complexes.

notes.A: A consistently prolonged PR interval with every P wave conducted describes first-degree atrioventricular delay.
notes.B: Progressive PR lengthening followed by a dropped beat characterises second-degree Mobitz type I block.
notes.C: Intermittent dropped QRS complexes with an otherwise fixed PR interval fit second-degree Mobitz type II block.
notes.D: Absent distinct P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm suggest atrial fibrillation rather than the stated pattern of complete block.

set-03-A-061.why: Stroke volume is blood ejected by one ventricle per beat, calculated as end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume. Around 70 millilitres is a typical resting adult estimate.

notes.A: Beats per minute measure heart rate. Stroke volume is measured in millilitres per beat.
notes.C: About five litres is close to a typical resting cardiac output over one minute, not the volume ejected in one beat.
notes.D: Half a litre is several times a typical resting stroke volume. The usual estimate is tens of millilitres per beat.
notes.E: Millimetres of mercury measure pressure, such as systolic arterial pressure. They are not units of volume.

set-03-A-062.why: The usual electrical axis is the mean frontal-plane direction of ventricular depolarisation. Net QRS deflections in limb leads, including leads I and aVF, can estimate it.

notes.A: Precordial leads view activation mainly in the horizontal plane. They are not used alone for the standard frontal QRS axis.
notes.C: P-wave deflections can define an atrial axis. The standard electrical axis here concerns ventricular depolarisation.
notes.D: T-wave deflections reflect ventricular repolarisation and can define a separate T-wave axis.
notes.E: Chest leads V1 and V2 provide local precordial information. The frontal-plane axis uses limb-lead projections.

set-03-A-063.why: The augmented limb leads aVR, aVL and aVF each compare a limb electrode with a reference formed from the other limb electrodes. They sample frontal-plane electrical activity.

notes.A: Leads I, II and III are standard bipolar limb leads. Each compares potentials between a selected pair of limbs.
notes.C: The augmented limb leads are correct, but adding the standard bipolar leads makes the group too broad.
notes.D: The chest leads are unipolar precordial leads, but ‘augmented’ identifies the three limb leads in this classification.
notes.E: The augmented set excludes the precordial chest leads, even though those also use a composite reference.

set-03-A-064.why: Mitral sounds are best heard at the cardiac apex, usually in the left fifth intercostal space near the midclavicular line. The precise position varies between individuals.

notes.A: The right second intercostal space next to the sternum is the usual aortic auscultation area.
notes.C: A right parasternal fourth-space point is not the usual apical projection for mitral sounds.
notes.D: The left second intercostal space at the sternal border is the usual pulmonary auscultation area.
notes.E: The left third parasternal space is an additional listening area for some murmurs. The mitral area lies lower and more lateral.

set-03-A-065.why: The ventricular plateau is sustained by slow inward calcium current through L-type channels balanced by outward potassium current. This prolongs depolarisation and helps trigger contraction.

notes.A: Potassium efflux provides outward current during the plateau and helps repolarise the cell when inward calcium current declines.
notes.B: Fast sodium influx produces the rapid upstroke. Those channels inactivate well before the plateau ends.
notes.C: The important potassium current during the plateau is outward, which counterbalances inward movement of positively charged calcium ions.
notes.E: Outward potassium current matters, but the major sustained inward current that defines the plateau is carried by calcium.

set-03-A-066.why: An extrasystole is a premature cardiac beat caused by an impulse arising before the next expected beat. It can transiently interrupt the rhythm without producing sustained tachycardia.

notes.A: A sustained rate above 200 describes a tachyarrhythmia rather than the isolated premature beat asked about here.
notes.B: Conduction problems alter propagation. A premature beat is defined by early impulse generation, even if its conduction is also abnormal.
notes.C: Altered excitability, automaticity or triggered activity can produce an early impulse. The premature contraction is its mechanical consequence.
notes.D: A premature contraction interrupts the expected rhythm, which describes the event. The combination also includes the electrical disturbance.

set-03-A-068.why: Kinins such as bradykinin generally promote vasodilatation through endothelial signalling, including nitric oxide and prostacyclin release. Several other listed mediators can constrict resistance vessels.

notes.A: Noradrenaline activates vascular alpha adrenergic receptors and commonly produces systemic arteriolar constriction.
notes.B: Adrenaline can cause alpha-mediated vasoconstriction, particularly at higher concentrations. Beta-2 vasodilatation can predominate in some beds.
notes.C: Serotonin can constrict some vessels through smooth muscle receptors. Its net effects depend on the vascular bed and endothelium.
notes.D: Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor in many vascular beds and helps raise systemic vascular resistance.

set-03-A-070.why: A pressure gradient across a vascular bed depends on flow and resistance. Minute ventilation is not a direct term in that relation, although breathing can indirectly affect haemodynamics.

notes.A: Cardiac output supplies systemic flow. For a given vascular resistance, greater flow requires a greater pressure gradient.
notes.C: Viscosity affects resistance for a given vessel geometry. This changes the pressure drop needed to sustain a specified flow.
notes.D: Total peripheral resistance is the pressure difference across the systemic circulation divided by systemic flow.
notes.E: Circulating volume can alter venous pressure, filling and cardiac output. These changes influence the pressure gradient indirectly.

set-03-A-071.why: After ejection ends, semilunar valves close while atrioventricular valves remain closed. Pressure falls at constant ventricular volume until the inflow valves open and ventricular filling starts.

notes.A: If both sets were open, the ventricle could exchange blood with atria or arteries and volume would not remain fixed.
notes.B: Open semilunar valves with closed atrioventricular valves describe ventricular ejection, which precedes the relaxation interval.
notes.C: Open atrioventricular valves indicate that filling has started. This occurs after isovolumetric relaxation ends.
notes.E: The combination of closed inflow and closed outflow valves is present among the choices for this phase.

set-03-A-072.why: The first heart sound occurs at the beginning of ventricular systole. Rising ventricular pressure closes the atrioventricular valves and produces vibrations of the associated cardiac structures.

notes.A: The timing is correct. Ventricular contraction raises pressure and triggers closure of the atrioventricular valves, which explains the sound.
notes.B: Mitral and tricuspid closure produce the main components of the first sound. Their closure occurs at the start of systole.
notes.C: Semilunar valve closure generates the second heart sound at the end of ejection.
notes.D: The valve association is correct, but closure occurs when ventricular systole begins rather than during ventricular diastole.

set-03-A-073.why: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Stroke volume can change when preload or afterload varies.by changing how much the ventricle fills and how easily it ejects.

notes.A: Vital capacity describes an exhalable lung volume. It does not enter the equation for cardiac output.
notes.B: Stroke volume gives output per beat. It must be combined with the rate to calculate volume per minute.
notes.C: Heart rate gives beats per minute. Cardiac output also depends on how much blood each beat ejects.
notes.D: Stroke volume can change when preload or afterload varies. The direct equation for cardiac output uses stroke volume and heart rate.

set-03-A-076.why: Heart rate is the number of cardiac cycles per minute. At 60 beats per minute, dividing 60 seconds by 60 cycles gives one second per cycle.

notes.A: A half-second cycle would correspond to 120 beats per minute, twice the stated rate.
notes.B: A cycle lasting 0.8 seconds would give 75 beats per minute rather than 60.
notes.D: A 0.2-second cycle would require 300 cycles per minute, far above the stated heart rate.
notes.E: One second is the duration calculated from the stated rate and appears explicitly among the choices.

set-03-A-077.why: Pulse pressure is the difference between the highest arterial pressure during systole and the lowest arterial pressure during diastole. It depends on stroke volume and arterial compliance.

notes.A: Pulse pressure is a difference rather than a pressure point between systolic and diastolic readings.
notes.B: An arithmetic average combines the two pressures by addition and division. Calculating pulse pressure instead requires subtraction.
notes.C: The value measures the excursion between peak and trough. It need not be a particular distance from either absolute reading.
notes.E: The familiar one-third approximation estimates mean arterial pressure by adding part of the pulse pressure to diastolic pressure.

set-03-A-078.why: Key cardiovascular control circuits lie in the medulla oblongata. They integrate afferent information and adjust autonomic output controlling heart rate, contractility and vascular tone.

notes.A: The hypothalamus influences autonomic responses during stress and temperature regulation. It modulates rather than houses the principal medullary reflex circuits.
notes.B: The mesencephalon is the midbrain. Major arterial baroreflex integration occurs farther caudally in the medulla.
notes.C: Cortical activity can affect autonomic output. The core cardiovascular reflex processing is carried out in the brainstem.
notes.E: Spinal cord segments carry sympathetic output toward the heart and vessels. Their activity is regulated by brainstem pathways.

set-03-A-079.why: Pulmonary circulation begins with right ventricular ejection into the pulmonary trunk and arteries. Blood reaches lung capillaries for gas exchange and returns to the left atrium.

notes.A: The right ventricle ejects into the pulmonary trunk. The aorta receives blood from the left ventricle.
notes.C: The right atrium passes blood into the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve rather than directly into the left ventricle.
notes.D: The right atrium passes blood to the right ventricle. That ventricle supplies the pressure for pulmonary arterial flow.
notes.E: The left ventricle ejects into the aorta and supplies systemic circulation. The right ventricle supplies the lungs.

set-03-A-080.why: Systemic circulation begins with left ventricular ejection through the aortic valve into the aorta. Systemic venous blood ultimately returns to the right atrium.

notes.B: The aorta receives blood directly from the left ventricle. Right ventricular output enters the pulmonary trunk.
notes.C: Right ventricular flow to the lungs describes pulmonary circulation rather than systemic arterial outflow.
notes.D: Pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium. This completes the pulmonary circuit.
notes.E: The right atrium receives systemic venous blood and passes it into the right ventricle before it reaches the lungs.

set-03-A-081.why: The cardiac cycle consists of electrical and mechanical events within a single heartbeat. Heart rate counts how many times that cycle occurs in one minute.

notes.A: An impulse begins in the sinoatrial node and propagates through atrial, conducting and ventricular tissue during each heartbeat.
notes.B: Valve positions change as pressure gradients reverse during the cycle, directing forward flow and preventing backflow.
notes.D: Pressure rises with contraction and falls with relaxation. These changing gradients drive flow and determine when valves move.
notes.E: Chamber volumes change during filling and ejection. Ventricular volume stays constant only during the isovolumetric phases.

set-03-A-082.why: Endothelial nitric oxide synthase produces nitric oxide in blood vessels. It diffuses into nearby smooth muscle and activates cyclic GMP signalling, relaxing the vessel.

notes.A: Antidiuretic hormone is synthesised in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. It has renal and vascular actions.
notes.B: Atrial natriuretic peptide is secreted mainly by stretched atrial myocytes. It is not the endothelial vasodilator in this item.
notes.C: Renin is released primarily by renal juxtaglomerular cells. Its downstream products help regulate pressure and salt balance.
notes.E: Adrenaline is released mainly by the adrenal medulla. It is a circulating hormone rather than the local endothelial mediator asked for.

set-03-A-083.why: Capillaries have a thin endothelial wall and provide a large surface area for exchange. Gases and small solutes move between blood and tissues across that short barrier.

notes.A: Arterioles chiefly control local resistance and delivery to downstream exchange vessels. Their smooth muscle can change lumen calibre.
notes.B: Arteries conduct and distribute blood under pressure. Their thicker walls are not the principal site of exchange.
notes.C: Veins return blood toward the heart and serve as a compliant reservoir. Most nutrient and gas transfer occurs before blood reaches them.
notes.E: Postcapillary venules can exchange fluid and allow leukocyte passage, but capillaries provide the principal surface for nutrient and gas exchange.

set-03-A-084.why: Within the physiological range of filling, an increase in initial myocardial fibre length increases active force. Length-dependent activation helps link ventricular preload to systolic performance.

notes.A: Pacemaker activity determines how often the heart beats. Initial fibre stretch has a direct effect on force at a given rate.
notes.B: The atrioventricular delay allows filling before contraction. It is timing rather than the muscle’s length–force relation.
notes.D: Breathing can influence venous return, but the immediate mechanical determinant described is initial cardiac fibre length.
notes.E: The ST segment reflects an electrical phase after ventricular depolarisation. It is not a measure of initial mechanical stretch.

set-03-A-085.why: The inferior vena cava collects systemic venous blood from structures below the diaphragm and enters the right atrium. Blood then crosses the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

notes.A: The left atrium receives pulmonary veins. Systemic caval return enters the opposite atrium.
notes.C: The aorta is the systemic arterial outlet from the left ventricle, not a destination for caval venous blood.
notes.D: The left ventricle is filled from the left atrium across the mitral valve. Caval flow reaches the right side first.
notes.E: Blood passes into the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve. The vena cava opens into the right atrium.

set-03-A-086.why: The sinoatrial node has the fastest normal spontaneous firing rate and initiates sinus rhythm. Downstream conducting tissues follow its timing unless a slower escape focus takes over.

notes.A: Purkinje fibres distribute ventricular activation and have latent automaticity. They normally follow impulses arriving from higher pacemakers.
notes.B: Bundle branches conduct impulses down the septum. They do not normally initiate the heartbeat.
notes.C: The His bundle carries excitation from the atrioventricular junction to the bundle branches, downstream of sinus initiation.
notes.D: The atrioventricular node delays impulses and can take part in an escape rhythm. It ordinarily follows sinoatrial activation.

set-03-A-087.why: The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve. It opens for flow from the right atrium into the right ventricle and closes during ventricular systole.

notes.A: The right and left atria are separated by the interatrial septum. A normal valve does not connect them.
notes.B: The ventricles are separated by the interventricular septum. The tricuspid valve is located at the right ventricular inflow.
notes.D: The mitral valve occupies the opening from left atrium to left ventricle. The tricuspid valve is on the right.
notes.E: The right ventricular outflow leads through the pulmonary valve to the pulmonary trunk. The aorta arises from the left ventricle.

set-03-A-088.why: Rising left ventricular pressure closes the mitral valve at the beginning of systole. The closed valve prevents reverse flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium.

notes.A: The normal forward direction during filling is from the left atrium into the left ventricle, when the mitral valve is open.
notes.C: The right atrium supplies the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve. The mitral valve lies on the left side.
notes.D: Flow from left ventricle to aorta passes through the aortic valve during ejection. The mitral valve guards the inlet.
notes.E: The right ventricle ejects through the pulmonary valve. The mitral valve has no direct role at that outflow.

set-03-A-089.why: The atrioventricular node is the principal slow-conducting segment between atria and ventricles. Its delay helps the atria contract and empty before ventricular systole begins.

notes.A: The sinoatrial node initiates the impulse. The characteristic delay between atrial and ventricular activation is at the atrioventricular node.
notes.B: Activation passes through atrial myocardium more rapidly than it travels through the atrioventricular node.
notes.C: Purkinje fibres have high conduction velocity, which helps activate the large ventricular myocardium in a coordinated sequence.
notes.E: The His bundle carries excitation rapidly from the atrioventricular node toward the ventricular bundle branches.

set-03-A-090.why: Gap junction channels at intercalated discs allow ionic current to pass between adjoining myocytes. Electrical coupling coordinates activity across many separate cells as a functional syncytium.

notes.A: Striations are produced by ordered sarcomeres. They help identify the contractile apparatus but do not conduct current between cells.
notes.B: Branching describes cell shape and contact geometry. Gap junction pores supply the low-resistance electrical connections.
notes.D: Desmosomes provide strong mechanical adhesion while the heart contracts. Gap junctions provide the path for intercellular current.
notes.E: Calcium activates contraction inside each myocyte. Its concentration alone does not create electrical continuity between cells.

set-03-A-092.why: Local vasodilator signals increase coronary flow when the myocardium is hypoxic and vascular reserve remains. Left ventricular inflow is ordinarily greatest during diastole, when compression is relieved.

notes.A: Early ventricular contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels and decreases left coronary flow, particularly near the subendocardium.
notes.C: Cooling lowers myocardial metabolic demand and generally reduces the signals that increase coronary flow.
notes.D: Parasympathetic stimulation usually slows the heart and can reduce demand. It does not reliably provide the metabolic stimulus of myocardial hypoxia.
notes.E: Atrioventricular block changes rhythm and ventricular rate. It does not consistently increase local coronary flow through metabolic vasodilatation.

set-03-A-093.why: Coronary flow closely tracks the myocardium’s oxygen demand. The heart already extracts much of the delivered oxygen, so increased work depends mainly on increasing local perfusion.

notes.B: Skin flow is strongly influenced by thermoregulation and sympathetic tone as well as local factors.
notes.C: Gland perfusion can rise with activity, but the category includes different organs. Coronary flow shows the classic close match to oxygen consumption.
notes.D: Pulmonary flow is set largely by right ventricular output. Regional distribution depends strongly on ventilation and alveolar oxygen.
notes.E: Renal perfusion is high relative to metabolic demand and is controlled substantially by myogenic and tubuloglomerular autoregulation.

set-03-A-094.why: Tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells restrict movement through intercellular spaces. These cells form the principal barrier and are supported by pericytes and nearby astrocyte endfeet.

notes.A: Oligodendrocytes form myelin around central axons. The barrier separating blood from brain interstitial fluid lies in capillary endothelium.
notes.B: Microglia are resident immune cells of the central nervous system. They do not form the endothelial seal.
notes.D: Ependyma lines ventricles. The distinct blood–cerebrospinal fluid barrier is mainly at choroid plexus epithelium, rather than typical ependyma.
notes.E: Most brain capillary endothelial cells lack fenestrations. The tight junctions and selective transcellular transport form the principal barrier.

set-03-A-095.why: The second heart sound, associated with aortic and pulmonary valve closure, is normally shorter and higher pitched than the first sound. It is often prominent at the base.

notes.A: The first sound generally has a longer, lower-pitched quality. The second is typically briefer and higher pitched.
notes.C: Atrioventricular valve closure is associated with the first sound. The second follows closure of the semilunar valves.
notes.D: The onset of ventricular systole produces the first sound. The second occurs near the end of ejection.
notes.E: The second sound is generally prominent over the base. The first sound is often more prominent over the apex.

set-03-A-096.why: During exercise, the pulmonary circulation accommodates greater flow by recruiting and distending vessels. These changes lower pulmonary vascular resistance despite the increase in pulmonary blood flow.

notes.A: The pulmonary pressure gradient is much smaller than the systemic gradient at comparable flow, indicating lower resistance.
notes.B: Low alveolar oxygen promotes local pulmonary vasoconstriction. This raises resistance in the affected vascular region.
notes.C: Flow divided by pressure difference is conductance. Vascular resistance is pressure difference divided by volume flow rate.
notes.E: Pulmonary vessels have autonomic innervation, but recruitment, distension and local oxygen effects are major determinants of resistance in this comparison.

set-03-A-097.why: Cerebral blood flow is strongly controlled by local metabolism, arterial carbon dioxide and autoregulation. The cerebral circulation is comparatively less dependent on sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone under ordinary conditions.

notes.B: Splanchnic vessels have substantial sympathetic tone and constrict during haemorrhage or other states requiring redistribution.
notes.C: Renal sympathetic activation can constrict resistance vessels, lower renal blood flow and promote renin release.
notes.D: Skin circulation is strongly controlled by sympathetic pathways, particularly across changes in body temperature and sympathetic drive.
notes.E: Skeletal muscle vessels receive sympathetic vasoconstrictor input. Local signals can attenuate that effect in actively contracting muscle.

set-03-A-099.why: During cuff deflation the first Korotkoff sounds indicate systolic pressure. Their later disappearance usually marks diastolic pressure, and the cuff bladder is sized to arm circumference.

notes.A: The arterial pulse beneath the cuff produces local tissue vibrations. Heart sounds are generated separately in the thorax.
notes.C: Diastolic pressure usually corresponds to the disappearance of sounds. The loudest sounds do not define that threshold.
notes.D: A palpable pulse can be detected only after sufficient flow has returned. Auscultatory readings can also be affected by an unrecognised gap.
notes.E: Wider cuff bladders are needed for larger arm circumferences. An oversized cuff on a small arm can underestimate pressure.

set-03-A-100.why: Ventricular myocardium is absolutely refractory from the start of depolarisation into repolarisation, because many fast sodium channels remain inactivated. Excitability returns gradually as those channels recover.

notes.A: Ventricular myocytes usually have a longer action potential and refractory period than atrial myocytes.
notes.B: The absolute refractory period overlaps much of ventricular contraction. It does not mainly coincide with the later relaxation phase.
notes.D: A stronger stimulus can elicit a response during relative refractoriness. Absolute refractoriness prevents re-excitation regardless of stimulus strength.
notes.E: Vagal effects are strongest in nodal and atrial tissue. Marked prolongation of ventricular absolute refractoriness is not its defining effect.

set-03-A-101.why: The Aschner–Dagnini or oculocardiac reflex is a trigeminovagal reflex. Sensory input from ocular structures can activate vagal outflow and slow the sinoatrial pacemaker.

notes.A: Goltz’s reflex classically describes a vagal cardiac response to abdominal visceral stimulation. The ocular afferent pathway has a different name.
notes.B: A pressor reflex raises arterial pressure through cardiovascular effectors. It does not name the ocular trigeminovagal response.
notes.C: The Bezold–Jarisch reflex involves cardiac sensory afferents. The oculocardiac reflex begins with sensory input from ocular structures.
notes.E: The response can lower heart rate or pressure, but ‘depressor reflex’ is a general description rather than the specific eponym.

set-03-A-102.why: Cycle duration equals 60 seconds divided by beats per minute. At 75 beats per minute, the interval between corresponding points on successive beats is 0.8 seconds.

notes.A: A one-second cycle corresponds to 60 beats per minute, which is slower than the stated rate.
notes.B: A cycle duration of 0.6 seconds would give 100 beats per minute rather than 75.
notes.C: A 1.2-second cycle is equivalent to 50 beats per minute, which is slower than the rate given.
notes.E: One and a half seconds per cycle would produce 40 beats per minute, substantially below the stated rate.

set-03-A-104.why: Sinoatrial nodal cells lack a stable resting membrane potential. Their diastolic depolarisation reaches threshold spontaneously, allowing them to generate impulses even without extrinsic autonomic input.

notes.A: The sinoatrial node is located in the right atrium near the superior vena cava. Its impulses spread to both atria.
notes.B: Sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres modulate the node. Its extrinsic innervation is autonomic rather than somatic.
notes.C: Denervated nodal cells still depolarise spontaneously. Neural input changes the rate and does not provide the initiating impulse.
notes.D: Excitation passes to the atrioventricular node through atrial conduction pathways. The Purkinje network distributes excitation within the ventricles.

set-03-A-105.why: The first heart sound occurs when rising ventricular pressure closes the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of systole. It accompanies early isovolumetric contraction.

notes.A: Aortic and pulmonary valve closure produces the second heart sound near the end of ventricular ejection.
notes.B: The P wave represents atrial electrical activation, which precedes the ventricular pressure rise and first sound.
notes.C: The immediate mechanical event is closure of the atrioventricular valves as ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure.
notes.E: The central venous a wave is produced by atrial contraction before ventricular systole and the first heart sound.

set-03-A-106.why: The long cardiac refractory period overlaps most of the contraction. This prevents repeated excitation from summating into tetany and preserves relaxation and filling between successive beats.

notes.A: Atrial and ventricular sequence depends on conduction timing, particularly the atrioventricular delay. Refractoriness prevents repeated excitation within a beat.
notes.B: Refractoriness limits re-excitation during systole. Filling depends on diastolic duration and opening of the inflow valves.
notes.C: Even during exercise, refractoriness limits temporal summation. The heart increases output by changing rate, filling and force.
notes.E: A refractory ventricle is temporarily less responsive to premature stimuli, and during absolute refractoriness it cannot be re-excited.

set-03-A-107.why: Greater left ventricular filling can increase end-diastolic fibre length. Within the physiological range, the Frank–Starling response increases active force at a given state of contractility.

notes.B: Higher extracellular potassium alters membrane potential and can impair excitation at marked elevations. It is not the normal preload stimulus.
notes.C: Lower extracellular calcium generally reduces calcium available for excitation–contraction coupling rather than increasing developed force.
notes.D: Magnesium changes can affect electrical stability and calcium handling. A fall is not the standard mechanism linking filling to force.
notes.E: Lower peripheral resistance can make ejection easier by reducing afterload. It does not increase initial stretch in the way greater filling does.

set-03-A-108.why: Cardiac parasympathetic activity slows the sinoatrial pacemaker through acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors. It can also increase the conduction delay through the atrioventricular node.

notes.A: Cardiac vagal activity primarily changes nodal behaviour. Hypertension is not the characteristic direct response.
notes.B: Tachycardia is a faster rate, whereas vagal input reduces the rate of spontaneous nodal firing.
notes.D: A longer filling interval can influence stroke volume indirectly. Bradycardia is the characteristic direct effect of cardiac vagal stimulation.
notes.E: Slowing of sinoatrial discharge is a recognised parasympathetic effect and has a corresponding choice.

set-03-A-109.why: Cardiac output is the volume pumped by either ventricle per minute. It equals stroke volume multiplied by heart rate and is normally expressed in litres per minute.

notes.B: A resting adult typically has output nearer five litres per minute. Two litres per minute is low for many adults.
notes.C: Ten litres per minute can occur at higher demand. It is above the standard value used for resting adult physiology.
notes.D: Cold exposure can affect haemodynamics through several reflex and metabolic pathways. An increase is not the defining behaviour of cardiac output.
notes.E: A denervated heart can increase output through increased filling and circulating catecholamines. The response loses rapid direct neural adjustments.

set-03-A-110.why: Raising the arm above heart level lowers local arterial pressure through the hydrostatic height difference. The brachial arterial pulse wave is a separate travelling pressure disturbance.

notes.A: The arterial pressure wave travels faster than the average movement of blood. Wave speed and flow velocity are distinct quantities.
notes.B: A stiffer arterial wall generally has lower compliance. For a given ejected volume, reduced compliance can increase pulse pressure.
notes.C: Distal occlusion stops downstream flow and alters reflections. It does not require a marked elevation of proximal mean pressure.
notes.E: Peripheral pulse pressure can exceed central aortic pulse pressure because of wave transmission and reflection along the arterial tree.

set-03-A-113.why: In healthy arteries pulse pressure often increases between the proximal aorta and peripheral muscular vessels. Changes in stiffness and wave reflections can amplify the systolic pressure excursion.

notes.A: The proximal aorta has abundant elastin. Farther away, distributing arteries are generally more muscular and less elastic.
notes.B: Smaller arterial size does not by itself establish more turbulence. Vessel diameter, flow velocity and viscosity all influence the tendency.
notes.D: Mean arterial pressure falls along the circuit as pressure energy is dissipated, even though the pulse amplitude can increase.
notes.E: Substantial oxygen exchange occurs mainly in the microcirculation. The pressure changes in distributing arteries do not imply major oxygen loss.

set-03-A-114.why: Stimulating cardiac vagal fibres slows sinoatrial pacemaking through muscarinic receptors. If stimulation is strong, it can also slow transmission through the atrioventricular node.

notes.A: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and removes vagal slowing. It commonly increases the heart rate rather than reducing it.
notes.C: Glucocorticoids affect metabolism and vascular responsiveness. They are not the usual immediate physiological signal for slowing sinus rate.
notes.D: Calcium influences excitation–contraction coupling and can affect rhythm. It is not the standard direct intervention for physiological vagal slowing.
notes.E: Adrenaline stimulates cardiac beta receptors, usually accelerating sinoatrial discharge and increasing myocardial force.

set-03-A-115.why: Excess aldosterone promotes renal sodium retention and can expand extracellular volume. These effects contribute to sustained systemic hypertension in conditions such as primary aldosteronism.

notes.A: Chronic alveolar hypoxia characteristically raises pulmonary vascular resistance. It more directly supports pulmonary rather than primary systemic hypertension in this comparison.
notes.C: Hyperinsulinaemia can accompany metabolic risk, but autonomous aldosterone excess is a direct established cause of secondary hypertension.
notes.D: Left ventricular hypertrophy is often a consequence of long-standing systemic pressure load. It is not itself the endocrine cause described here.
notes.E: Ventricular fibrillation prevents effective ventricular ejection. Arterial pressure collapses instead of rising from an effective rapid output.

set-03-A-116.why: During diastole arterial pressure falls as blood runs into peripheral vessels. Peripheral vascular resistance helps determine how rapidly that runoff occurs and how much pressure is maintained.

notes.A: Blood volume affects filling and pressure overall. It does not specifically describe resistance to diastolic runoff from the arterial compartment.
notes.B: Viscosity influences vascular resistance. The overall resistance of peripheral beds is the more direct determinant in this comparison.
notes.C: Ventricular ejection produces the arterial pressure rise and determines the amount ejected per beat. The rate of diastolic runoff depends mainly on vascular resistance and arterial compliance.
notes.E: Vessel length contributes to resistance but usually does not change quickly. Peripheral resistance integrates length, calibre and other factors.

set-03-A-117.why: During atrial fibrillation, atrial activity is rapid and disorganised. The atrioventricular node conducts only some of those impulses, so ventricular activation is slower and usually irregular.

notes.A: Discrete P waves are absent, but fibrillatory activity can be visible in the baseline. The atria still generate electrical activity.
notes.C: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia depends on sinus-driven beats. Ventricular irregularity during atrial fibrillation instead reflects variable conduction.
notes.D: Atrial electrical activity can be several hundred impulses per minute. The atrioventricular node normally limits the number reaching the ventricles.
notes.E: QRS complexes can remain narrow when ventricular conduction is otherwise normal. A wide or abnormal complex is not required.

set-03-A-118.why: Fenestrated capillary endothelium contains pores that facilitate rapid exchange of water and small solutes. The capillary wall remains thin and lacks a continuous smooth muscle coat.

notes.B: Continuous capillaries are more widespread. Fenestrated capillaries specialise in exchange in tissues such as renal glomeruli and endocrine organs.
notes.C: Exchange follows pressure and concentration gradients and can occur in either direction. Fenestrations do not form one-way valves.
notes.D: Capillaries have an endothelial wall and basal lamina. They lack the smooth muscle coat characteristic of arterioles.
notes.E: Glomerular capillaries are classically fenestrated. Hepatic sinusoids also have pores but are conventionally classified as discontinuous capillaries.

set-03-A-119.why: At ordinary resting rates, mean arterial pressure can be estimated as diastolic pressure plus one-third of pulse pressure. The estimate reflects the relatively longer time spent in diastole.

notes.A: At ordinary resting rates, pressure spends more time lower in the cycle, so the mean is usually closer to diastolic pressure.
notes.B: The simple arithmetic average weights peak and trough equally. The actual mean is a time average over the pressure waveform.
notes.D: Subtracting diastolic pressure from systolic pressure gives pulse pressure, which measures the size of the pressure excursion.
notes.E: Adding a fraction of diastolic pressure to systolic pressure can exceed the peak. The mean lies between systolic and diastolic pressures.

set-03-A-120.why: Cardiac output is the volume ejected by one ventricle per unit time. It is obtained by multiplying the amount ejected per beat by beats per minute.

notes.A: Volume ejected in one beat is stroke volume. To obtain cardiac output it must be multiplied by heart rate.
notes.B: The ventricles pump in series, so adding their outputs would count flow through both sides of the same circulation twice.
notes.D: End-diastolic volume is the amount in the ventricle before contraction, not the volume delivered over a minute.
notes.E: End-systolic volume is what remains after ejection. Cardiac output measures the amount ejected per minute.

set-03-A-121.why: Pulse-wave velocity describes propagation of pressure along arterial walls. It depends strongly on wall stiffness and geometry, so it differs between vascular segments and changes with age.

notes.A: Blood flow velocity is the motion of fluid. The arterial pulse is a pressure disturbance that can travel much faster.
notes.B: Arterial segments differ in calibre and stiffness. Their pulse waves therefore do not all travel at the same speed.
notes.D: Arterial stiffness typically increases with age, which raises pulse-wave velocity even if mean blood flow is unchanged.
notes.E: Peripheral muscular arteries are often less distensible than the proximal aorta. Their pulse-wave speeds need not be lower.

set-03-A-122.why: Stiffer arteries expand less for a given stroke volume. This tends to increase systolic pressure and widen pulse pressure, particularly as large elastic arteries stiffen with age.

notes.A: Hardening decreases arterial compliance. More pressure is required to produce the same change in arterial volume.
notes.C: Diastolic pressure does not necessarily rise with large-artery stiffness. Reduced elastic buffering commonly widens pulse pressure instead.
notes.D: Total peripheral resistance is governed mainly by resistance-vessel calibre. Large-artery stiffness acts strongly on pulsatile pressure and ventricular load.
notes.E: Breathing frequency is regulated by respiratory neural and chemical feedback. It is not the principal consequence of arterial stiffening.

set-03-A-123.why: Left ventricular failure can raise left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure. The rise is transmitted to pulmonary capillaries, increasing the hydrostatic drive for pulmonary oedema.

notes.A: Right atrial pressure can rise if right-sided dysfunction develops later. The more direct effect of left ventricular failure is pulmonary congestion.
notes.B: Ejection fraction can be reduced or preserved in left-sided heart failure. It does not characteristically increase as the ventricle fails.
notes.D: Pulmonary congestion and interstitial oedema make lungs harder to inflate. Lung compliance generally falls rather than increases.
notes.E: Pulmonary oedema is driven by elevated capillary pressure. Standing is not the characteristic condition that causes it in left ventricular failure.

set-03-A-124.why: Capillary fluid transfer depends on hydrostatic and oncotic forces across the microvascular barrier. Intrapleural pressure is not a separate direct force in the general transcapillary balance.

notes.A: Capillary blood pressure supplies an outward hydrostatic force that helps drive fluid into the interstitial compartment.
notes.B: Plasma proteins produce colloid osmotic pressure, which opposes outward fluid movement across the endothelial barrier.
notes.D: Hydrostatic pressure in surrounding tissue acts on the outside of the capillary and enters the pressure difference across its wall.
notes.E: The classical Starling model includes interstitial oncotic pressure. The revised model considers the protein concentration beneath the endothelial glycocalyx.

set-03-A-125.why: The vagus normally restrains sinoatrial pacemaker rate at rest. Blocking vagal input removes that muscarinic inhibition, allowing the heart rate to rise toward its intrinsic value.

notes.A: A slower rate would follow increased vagal stimulation. Removing that influence produces the opposite pacemaker response.
notes.B: Stroke volume may change with filling time, but it is not the direct predictable result of loss of vagal input.
notes.C: Cardiac output depends on both rate and stroke volume. A fall is not the inevitable response to vagal blockade.
notes.E: Even though the heart has intrinsic automaticity, removing a tonic inhibitory input changes how rapidly it discharges.

set-03-A-126.why: Slow inward calcium current through L-type channels helps sustain the plateau in a contractile myocyte. It counterbalances outward potassium current and contributes to excitation–contraction coupling.

notes.A: Sodium influx produces the rapid upstroke in working ventricular cells. It is not the principal inward current sustaining the plateau.
notes.C: Outward potassium currents help repolarise the membrane. During the plateau they are balanced in part by inward calcium current.
notes.D: Fast sodium channels increase sodium permeability during phase zero and then inactivate. The plateau follows that brief event.
notes.E: The plateau depends on continued calcium entry. Declining inward current helps allow outward potassium current to repolarise the cell.
